name: Python in Depth
audience: Experienced developers who already write Python and want to understand how it really works: the object model, the interpreter, concurrency and modern typing.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of code-reading, predict-the-output, debugging and design questions.

domains.name: The data model and object system
domains.summary: Special methods and protocols, the __eq__/__hash__ contract, attribute lookup and descriptors, MRO and cooperative super(), and how classes are created with metaclasses, __init_subclass__ and __set_name__.

domains.name: Functions, scopes, iterators and generators
domains.summary: LEGB scoping, closures and late binding, default arguments and decorators. Also covers the iterator protocol, generators with send and yield from, lazy itertools pipelines and functools tools such as lru_cache and singledispatch.

domains.name: Memory, the interpreter and the import system
domains.summary: Reference counting and the cyclic garbage collector, copies and identity, bytecode and the CPython interpreter, the GIL, and how imports, packages and circular imports really work.

domains.name: Concurrency and asyncio
domains.summary: Choosing between threads, processes and asyncio, concurrent.futures, and asyncio in depth: tasks, TaskGroup, timeouts, cancellation and exception groups. Also covers common asyncio bugs and what is and is not thread-safe in CPython.

domains.name: Modern typing and language features
domains.summary: Generics and PEP 695 syntax, variance, Protocol, TypedDict, overload, Self and ParamSpec as of Python 3.13. Also covers dataclasses versus NamedTuple, structural pattern matching, enums, context managers and exception design.

domains.name: Performance, testing and packaging
domains.summary: The cost model of built-in types and measuring with timeit, cProfile and tracemalloc. Also covers testing with pytest and unittest.mock, packaging with pyproject.toml, and designing and deprecating a library's public API.

scenarios.title: Debugging a production memory leak
scenarios.description: A long-running service keeps growing. Trace reference cycles, caches and lingering references with gc, weakref and tracemalloc, and fix the leak without breaking behaviour.

scenarios.title: Designing a plugin framework
scenarios.description: Let third parties register plugins by subclassing, with validation at class creation. Choose between __init_subclass__, descriptors, ABCs and metaclasses.

scenarios.title: Speeding up a slow data pipeline
scenarios.description: Profile before optimising, pick the right data structures and generators, and decide whether threads, processes or vectorised code will actually help under the GIL.

scenarios.title: Moving a sync service to asyncio
scenarios.description: Port blocking I/O code to asyncio with TaskGroup, timeouts and correct cancellation, without blocking the event loop or losing tasks.

scenarios.title: Reviewing a library's public API
scenarios.description: Check signatures, typing, deprecation warnings, tests and packaging metadata so the library can evolve without breaking its callers.

lessons.title: Special methods and protocols
lessons.summary: Python operators and built-ins such as `len()`, `==`, `hash()` and `in` are thin wrappers over special ("dunder") methods. Knowing exactly which method each one calls, and what it falls back to, explains most surprising behaviour in user-defined classes.

sections.heading: How built-ins find special methods
sections.body:
The data model reference describes special methods as the hooks Python calls for operators and built-ins: `len(x)` calls `type(x).__len__(x)`, `a + b` tries `type(a).__add__(a, b)`, and so on.

Two consequences follow from the word **type** in that sentence:

- **Implicit lookup goes to the class, not the instance.** Assigning `obj.__len__ = lambda: 5` has no effect on `len(obj)`; it raises `TypeError` if the class has no `__len__`.
- **Implicit lookup also bypasses `__getattribute__`.** A logging `__getattribute__` will not see the `__len__` lookup made by `len()`.

The reference explains that this is deliberate: it keeps lookups fast and makes `hash(int)` and `repr(int)` refer to the metaclass methods rather than the instance methods.

sections.heading: __repr__ and __str__
sections.body:
- `__repr__` is the "official" representation, aimed at developers. Ideally it looks like a valid expression that would recreate the object; if that is impractical it should be an informative string like `<Order id=42>`.
- `__str__` is the "informal", user-facing representation used by `str()`, `print()` and `format()`.
- If a class defines only `__repr__`, `str()` falls back to it. The reverse is not true.
- Containers show their elements with `repr()`, so `print([order])` uses `Order.__repr__` even if `__str__` exists.

Rule of thumb: always define `__repr__` for classes you will debug; add `__str__` only if end users need a different text.

sections.heading: The __eq__ and __hash__ contract
Rich comparison and NotImplemented
sections.body:
The six rich comparison methods are `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__eq__`, `__ne__`, `__gt__` and `__ge__`.

- Return the singleton `NotImplemented` (do not raise, do not return `False`) when you do not know how to compare with the other operand. Python then tries the **reflected** method on the other operand: `__lt__` reflects to `__gt__`, `__eq__` to `__eq__`.
- If both sides return `NotImplemented`, `==` falls back to identity (`a is b`), while `<` raises `TypeError`.
- By default `__ne__` delegates to `__eq__` and inverts the result unless it is `NotImplemented`.
- `functools.total_ordering` fills in the missing ordering methods if the class defines `__eq__` and one of `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__` or `__ge__`. The functools docs note the derived methods are slower than hand-written ones.

Returning `False` instead of `NotImplemented` silently blocks the other operand from answering, which breaks comparisons with types written by someone else.

sections.heading: Container and numeric protocols
sections.body:
**Containers.** `__len__`, `__getitem__`, `__setitem__`, `__delitem__`, `__iter__` and `__contains__` make an object behave like a sequence or mapping.

- `in` uses `__contains__` if present; otherwise it iterates with `__iter__`; otherwise it falls back to the old sequence protocol, calling `__getitem__` with 0, 1, 2, ... until `IndexError`.
- `iter()` has the same `__getitem__` fallback, which is why a class with only `__getitem__` works in a `for` loop.
- Subclassing an ABC from `collections.abc` (see the inheritance lesson) gives you the remaining methods for free.

**Numbers.** `a + b` tries `a.__add__(b)`; if that returns `NotImplemented` (and the types differ), Python tries `b.__radd__(a)`.

- If the right operand's type is a **subclass** of the left operand's type and provides a different reflected method, the reflected method is tried first, so subclasses can override behaviour.
- Implement `__radd__` so that `sum()` works: `sum()` starts from `0`, so the first step is `0 + obj`.
- `a += b` tries `__iadd__` first; if it is missing, Python falls back to `a = a + b`, rebinding the name to a new object.

sections.heading: Truthiness: __bool__ and __len__
sections.body:
`bool(x)` calls `__bool__`, which must return a real `bool` (returning `1` raises `TypeError`). If `__bool__` is missing, Python calls `__len__` and treats zero as false. If neither exists, every instance is truthy.

This is why an empty custom collection that defines `__len__` is falsy in `if items:`, and why `if obj:` is the wrong way to test `obj is not None` for such classes.

keyPoints: Built-ins look up special methods on the type, not the instance, and skip `__getattribute__`.
`str()` falls back to `__repr__`; containers always use `repr()` of their elements.
Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` sets `__hash__` to None; equal objects must hash equal.
Return `NotImplemented` from binary and comparison methods so the other operand can try.
`in` and `iter()` fall back from `__contains__` to `__iter__` to `__getitem__`.
`bool()` uses `__bool__`, then `__len__`, else True.

gotchas.trap: Return False from `__eq__` when the other object has an unknown type.
gotchas.correct: Return `NotImplemented` so the reflected method gets a chance; `==` then falls back to identity if neither side knows.

gotchas.trap: Patch `obj.__len__` on an instance to change `len(obj)`.
gotchas.correct: Special methods are looked up on the type; define or change them on the class.

gotchas.trap: Hash every attribute, including mutable ones, to make a class hashable.
gotchas.correct: Hash exactly the immutable fields that `__eq__` compares, and only if they never change while stored.

lessons.lab: Write a `Money(amount, currency)` class with `__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__hash__`, `__add__` and `__radd__`. Check that `{Money(1, "EUR"), Money(1, "EUR")}` has one element, that `sum([Money(1, "EUR"), Money(2, "EUR")])` works, and that `Money(1, "EUR") == 1` is False without raising.

lessons.title: Attribute lookup, descriptors and __slots__
lessons.summary: `obj.name` is not a dictionary lookup. It is a precedence algorithm over the class MRO and the instance `__dict__`, driven by descriptors. Properties, methods, `classmethod`, `staticmethod` and `__slots__` are all built on it.

sections.heading: Instance and class dictionaries
sections.body:
Most instances store their attributes in `obj.__dict__`; classes store methods and class attributes in `Class.__dict__` (a read-only mapping proxy).

Reading `obj.x` eventually checks the instance dict and then the classes along `type(obj).__mro__`. Writing `obj.x = v` normally puts `x` in the instance dict, which is why assigning to an attribute that also exists on the class **shadows** the class attribute for that one instance.

```python
class Config:
    retries = 3          # shared class attribute
c = Config()
c.retries = 5            # new entry in c.__dict__
Config.retries           # still 3
```

sections.heading: The lookup precedence
sections.body:
`object.__getattribute__` implements this order for `obj.x` (the descriptor guide gives a pure-Python equivalent):

1. Find `x` on the type by walking the MRO. If it is a **data descriptor** (it defines `__set__` or `__delete__`), call its `__get__` and stop.
2. Otherwise, if `x` is in the **instance `__dict__`**, return that value.
3. Otherwise, if the class attribute is a **non-data descriptor** (only `__get__`), call its `__get__`; if it is a plain value, return it.
4. Otherwise raise `AttributeError`, which triggers `__getattr__` if the class defines one.

So data descriptors beat the instance dict, and the instance dict beats non-data descriptors and plain class attributes.

sections.heading: __getattr__ versus __getattribute__
Descriptors, functions and property
__slots__
sections.body:
Declaring `__slots__ = ('x', 'y')` makes the class store those attributes in fixed slots implemented as descriptors, instead of a per-instance `__dict__`.

- **Benefits:** smaller instances and faster attribute access, useful when you create millions of objects.
- **Costs:** you cannot add attributes not listed in `__slots__` (`AttributeError: ... no __dict__ for setting new attributes`); there is no `__weakref__` unless you list it; tools that need `__dict__` (such as `cached_property`) fail.
- A name cannot be both a slot and a class attribute: `ValueError: 'x' in __slots__ conflicts with class variable`. Put defaults in `__init__`.
- A subclass that does not declare `__slots__` gets a `__dict__` again, so the saving only holds if every class in the hierarchy declares slots.
- `dataclass(slots=True)` (3.10+) generates slots for you.

keyPoints: Data descriptor > instance `__dict__` > non-data descriptor or class attribute.
`__getattr__` is a fallback for failed lookups; `__getattribute__` intercepts every lookup.
Functions are non-data descriptors, which is how bound methods are created.
`property` is always a data descriptor; `cached_property` is a non-data descriptor that writes to the instance dict.
`__slots__` removes the per-instance dict: smaller and faster, but no new attributes.

gotchas.trap: Use `__getattribute__` to supply defaults for missing attributes.
gotchas.correct: Use `__getattr__`, which runs only when normal lookup fails.

gotchas.trap: Assume an instance attribute always wins over the class.
gotchas.correct: A data descriptor such as a property on the class wins over the instance `__dict__`.

gotchas.trap: Add `__slots__` to a base class and expect all subclasses to be dict-free.
gotchas.correct: Each subclass must declare its own `__slots__` or it regains a `__dict__`.

lessons.lab: Implement the `Positive` descriptor above, use it for two attributes of a class, and confirm that the error names the right attribute. Then add `__slots__` for the private names and measure `sys.getsizeof` of an instance with and without slots.

lessons.title: Inheritance: MRO, super() and ABCs
lessons.summary: Multiple inheritance in Python is predictable because every class has a single linear method resolution order (MRO) computed with C3. `super()` walks that order, which is what makes cooperative mixins work, and abstract base classes add interface checks on top.

sections.heading: MRO and C3 linearization
sections.body:
Every class has `__mro__`, a tuple listing the class, then its bases, ending in `object`. Attribute lookup and `super()` both follow it.

C3 linearization guarantees that:

- a class comes before its bases;
- the order of bases in the `class` statement is preserved (local precedence);
- each class's own MRO is respected (monotonicity).

```python
class O: pass
class X(O): pass
class Y(O): pass
class Z(X, Y): pass
[c.__name__ for c in Z.__mro__]   # ['Z', 'X', 'Y', 'O', 'object']
```

In the diamond, the shared base `O` appears **once**, after both `X` and `Y`. If no order satisfies the constraints (for example `class A(X, Y)`, `class B(Y, X)`, then `class C(A, B)`), class creation fails with `TypeError: Cannot create a consistent method resolution order (MRO)`.

sections.heading: Cooperative super()
Mixins
sections.body:
A mixin is a small class that adds one capability (`JSONMixin`, `ReprMixin`) and is not meant to be instantiated alone.

- Put mixins **to the left** of the main base class: `class Order(LoggingMixin, Model)`. The MRO then puts the mixin's methods first, and its `super()` calls reach `Model`.
- Keep mixins stateless or initialise state cooperatively with `**kwargs`.
- Prefer composition when the "mixin" needs lots of configuration or its own invariants.

sections.heading: Abstract base classes
sections.body:
`abc.ABC` (or `metaclass=ABCMeta`) plus `@abstractmethod` declares an interface (PEP 3119).

- A class with any unimplemented abstract method cannot be instantiated: `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...`. The check happens at **instantiation**, not at class definition.
- `Base.register(Other)` makes `Other` a **virtual subclass**: `isinstance` and `issubclass` return True, but `Other` inherits nothing from `Base` and its methods are not checked.
- `__subclasshook__` lets an ABC accept classes by structure; `collections.abc.Iterable` recognises any class with `__iter__`.
- The ABCs in `collections.abc` supply **mixin methods**: subclass `Mapping` and implement `__getitem__`, `__iter__` and `__len__`, and you get `__contains__`, `keys`, `items`, `values`, `get`, `__eq__` and `__ne__`.

Use ABCs when you control the hierarchy and want instantiation-time checks; consider `typing.Protocol` (covered in the typing domain) for structural typing without inheritance.

keyPoints: Every class has one MRO (`__mro__`) computed by C3; shared bases appear once, after all their subclasses.
Inconsistent base orders raise `TypeError` at class creation.
`super()` follows the MRO of `type(self)`, so every method in a cooperative chain must call it and forward `**kwargs`.
Abstract methods are enforced at instantiation; `register()` creates unchecked virtual subclasses.
`collections.abc` ABCs provide mixin methods once you implement the abstract ones.

gotchas.trap: `super()` calls the parent class.
gotchas.correct: It calls the next class in the MRO of the instance type, which may be a sibling.

gotchas.trap: Calling `Base.__init__(self)` directly is equivalent to `super().__init__()`.
gotchas.correct: Direct calls skip cooperative siblings and can run a shared base twice.

gotchas.trap: A registered virtual subclass must implement the abstract methods.
gotchas.correct: `register()` performs no checks and adds no methods.

lessons.lab: Build the `Left/Right/Both` diamond, print `Both.__mro__`, and log each `__init__`. Then replace one `super()` call with a direct `Base.__init__(self)` call and observe which initialiser is skipped.

lessons.title: Class creation: type, metaclasses and hooks
lessons.summary: A `class` statement is executable code that builds a namespace and passes it to a metaclass, by default `type`. Python 3.6 (PEP 487) added `__init_subclass__` and `__set_name__`, which cover most jobs that used to need a custom metaclass.

sections.heading: What a class statement does
sections.body:
The data model reference lists the steps:

1. Resolve the bases (including any `__mro_entries__`).
2. Determine the metaclass: an explicit `metaclass=` keyword, otherwise the most derived metaclass among the bases, otherwise `type`.
3. Prepare the namespace with `metaclass.__prepare__(name, bases, **kwargs)` (a plain dict by default).
4. Execute the class body in that namespace.
5. Create the class with `metaclass(name, bases, namespace, **kwargs)`. During this, `type.__new__` calls `__set_name__` on attributes that define it, then calls `__init_subclass__` on the parent.
6. Apply class decorators, bottom-up.

Because `type` is itself a class, `type(name, bases, dict)` builds a class dynamically: `Point = type('Point', (object,), {'x': 0})`.

sections.heading: Metaclasses
__init_subclass__
__set_name__
sections.body:
When a class is created, `type.__new__` calls `attr.__set_name__(owner, name)` for every attribute in the class body that defines it. Descriptors use this to learn their own attribute name, so you can write `price = Positive()` instead of `price = Positive('price')`.

The hook runs only at class creation. Attaching a descriptor later with `setattr(Cls, 'x', Desc())` does **not** call it; call it yourself if needed.

With the default metaclass, `type.__new__` calls every `__set_name__` before it calls the parent's `__init_subclass__`, so the latter can see fully named descriptors.

sections.heading: Class decorators and choosing a tool
sections.body:
A class decorator is a function that receives the finished class and returns it (or a replacement). `@dataclass` and `@functools.total_ordering` are class decorators.

- A decorator applies to **one class**; subclasses do not re-run it, although they inherit any attributes it set.
- `__init_subclass__` applies to **all subclasses** of the base automatically.
- A metaclass applies to all subclasses **and** controls the class object itself.

Pick the least powerful tool that works: a decorator for one-off transformations, `__init_subclass__` for registries and subclass validation, `__set_name__` for self-naming descriptors, and a metaclass only for namespace preparation or class-level operators.

keyPoints: The class body runs first; then the metaclass (default `type`) builds the class.
`type(name, bases, ns)` creates classes dynamically.
`__set_name__` runs for class-body attributes during class creation, then `__init_subclass__` runs on the parent.
`__init_subclass__` is inherited and receives class keyword arguments.
Class decorators affect one class; metaclasses propagate and can conflict.

gotchas.trap: Write a metaclass to register every subclass.
gotchas.correct: Use `__init_subclass__` (PEP 487); it is simpler and avoids metaclass conflicts.

gotchas.trap: Expect `__set_name__` to run when a descriptor is attached with `setattr` after class creation.
gotchas.correct: It runs only during class creation; call it manually otherwise.

gotchas.trap: Assume a class decorator applies to subclasses.
gotchas.correct: Decorators run once on the decorated class; use `__init_subclass__` for per-subclass behaviour.

lessons.lab: Build a plugin registry three ways: a class decorator, `__init_subclass__` and a metaclass. Subclass a registered plugin and note which approach registers the grandchild automatically, then try combining your metaclass-based base with an `abc.ABC` class and read the error.

lessons.title: Callables, methods and object identity
lessons.summary: Methods are functions turned into bound methods by the descriptor protocol; `staticmethod` and `classmethod` change what gets bound. Identity (`is`) and equality (`==`) are different questions, and the cases where `is` seems to work on values are CPython caching details.

sections.heading: Bound methods
sections.body:
Accessing `obj.method` calls the function's `__get__`, which returns a new **bound method** object packaging the function and `obj`. Accessing `Class.method` returns the plain function.

```python
class Button:
    def click(self): ...
b = Button()
b.click is b.click    # False: a fresh bound method each access
b.click == b.click    # True: same function, same instance
```

This matters when you register and later unregister callbacks: compare with `==`, or keep a reference to the bound method you registered. A bound method also holds a strong reference to its instance (`b.click.__self__`).

sections.heading: staticmethod, classmethod and __call__
sections.body:
- `@staticmethod` removes binding: the function receives no implicit first argument. Use it for helpers that logically belong to the class. Since 3.10 a staticmethod object is also directly callable.
- `@classmethod` binds the **class** (`cls`) instead of the instance, even when called on an instance. It is the idiom for alternative constructors: `cls(...)` builds the right subclass when called as `Sub.from_json(...)`.
- In 3.13, class methods can no longer wrap other descriptors such as `property`; that chaining was deprecated in 3.11.
- Any object whose class defines `__call__` is callable; `callable(x)` checks for it. Classes are callable because their metaclass (`type`) defines `__call__`, which runs `__new__` and then `__init__`.

sections.heading: is versus ==
sections.body:
- `a is b` tests **identity**: the same object. It cannot be overridden.
- `a == b` tests **equality** through `__eq__`.
- Use `is` for singletons: `None`, `True`/`False` (rarely needed), `NotImplemented`, `Ellipsis` and sentinel objects you create with `object()`. Use `==` for everything else.
- Built-in containers compare elements with an identity check first, so `nan = float('nan'); [nan] == [nan]` is True even though `nan == nan` is False.
- CPython emits a `SyntaxWarning` for `x is 1` or `x is "a"`, because comparing to a literal with `is` is almost always a bug.

sections.heading: Interning and caching are CPython details
Enum members and identity
sections.body: Enum members are singletons, so `status is Status.ACTIVE` is correct and idiomatic. A member defined with a value already used becomes an **alias**: `Color.CRIMSON is Color.RED` is True and iterating `Color` skips aliases. Use `@enum.unique` to forbid aliases.

keyPoints: `obj.method` creates a new bound method each time; compare bound methods with `==`.
`classmethod` binds the class and suits alternative constructors; `staticmethod` binds nothing.
Use `is` only for singletons and sentinels; use `==` for values.
Small-int caching and string interning are CPython implementation details.
Enum members are singletons; duplicate values create aliases.

gotchas.trap: `x is 1000` works because ints are cached.
gotchas.correct: Only -5 to 256 are cached in CPython, and even that is not guaranteed; use `==`.

gotchas.trap: Unregister a callback by filtering with `s is not obj.handler`.
gotchas.correct: Each access creates a new bound method, so identity never matches; compare with `==` or `!=` (or use `list.remove`, which uses equality).

gotchas.trap: Hard-code the class name in an alternative constructor: `return Order(...)`.
gotchas.correct: Use `@classmethod` and `cls(...)` so subclasses get instances of themselves.

lessons.lab: In a REPL, compare `a is b` and `a == b` for ints built with `int()` from strings "256" and "257", for strings built at runtime, and for two accesses of the same bound method. Then write a `Temperature.from_fahrenheit` classmethod and check it returns a subclass instance when called on a subclass.

lessons.title: Scopes, closures and late binding
lessons.summary: How Python decides which binding a name refers to, why closures see the latest value of a variable, and why default arguments are evaluated only once.

sections.heading: LEGB name resolution
sections.body:
When a name is read, Python looks in the **L**ocal scope, then any **E**nclosing function scopes, then the module's **G**lobal namespace, then **B**uiltins. The first binding found wins.

The important part is that scope is decided **at compile time**, from where assignments occur in the source, not at call time from whoever called the function. A function never sees its caller's local variables.

sections.heading: Assignment makes a name local
sections.body:
If a name is bound anywhere in a function body (by `=`, `+=`, `for`, `import`, `def`, `with ... as`, `except ... as`), it is local for the **whole** body. Reading it before the assignment raises `UnboundLocalError` (a subclass of `NameError`):

```python
total = 0
def add(n):
    total += n      # UnboundLocalError: total is local here
    return total
```

Reading a global is fine; only rebinding it needs a declaration.

sections.heading: global and nonlocal
sections.body:
`global x` makes assignments to `x` rebind the module-level name. `nonlocal x` makes them rebind the nearest **enclosing function** binding; it never reaches module globals, and declaring a `nonlocal` name with no enclosing function binding is a `SyntaxError`.

```python
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc
```

Each call to `make_counter()` creates a fresh cell for `count`, so counters are independent. The cells are visible on `inc.__closure__`.

sections.heading: Closures bind variables, not values
sections.body:
A closure keeps a reference to the variable (the cell), not a snapshot of its value. The value is looked up when the inner function **runs**. That is why

```python
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]      # [2, 2, 2]
```

All three lambdas share the one `i`, which is 2 when they are finally called. Fix it by binding the current value at creation time: `lambda i=i: i`, or `functools.partial(func, i)`.

sections.heading: Default arguments are evaluated once
sections.body:
Default values are evaluated **once, when the `def` statement executes**, and the same object is reused for every call. A mutable default therefore accumulates state:

```python
def append_to(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
append_to(1); append_to(1)   # [1, 1]
```

Writing `bucket=list()` does not help, because `list()` is also evaluated only once. The idiom is a `None` sentinel: `def append_to(item, bucket=None): if bucket is None: bucket = []`.

sections.heading: Class bodies and locals() in 3.13
sections.body:
A class body is a scope, but it is **not** an enclosing scope for functions or comprehensions defined inside it. Methods must use `self.attr` or `ClassName.attr`, and a comprehension in a class body cannot see class-level names (other than the outermost iterable).

In 3.13 (PEP 667), `locals()` inside a function returns an independent **snapshot**. Writing to that dict never changes the function's local variables.

keyPoints: Scope is decided at compile time from where names are assigned; lookup order is Local, Enclosing, Global, Builtins.
Any assignment to a name in a function makes it local for the entire function body.
nonlocal rebinds an enclosing function variable; global rebinds a module variable.
Closures capture variables, so loop-created lambdas see the final loop value unless you bind it with a default or partial.
Default values are evaluated once at def time; use None as the sentinel for mutable defaults.

gotchas.trap: Python looks up a missing local in the calling function's variables.
gotchas.correct: Scoping is lexical. A function sees its own locals, enclosing function definitions, module globals and builtins, never its caller's locals.

gotchas.trap: bucket=list() gives each call a fresh list.
gotchas.correct: The default expression runs once at def time, whatever it is. Use bucket=None and create the list in the body.

gotchas.trap: nonlocal can be used to rebind a module-level variable.
gotchas.correct: nonlocal only targets enclosing function scopes; use global for module-level names.

lessons.lab: Write a function that builds a list of three callbacks in a loop and prints what each returns. Fix the late-binding bug twice, once with a default argument and once with functools.partial. Then write a counter factory with nonlocal and confirm two counters are independent by inspecting __closure__.

lessons.title: Decorators: wraps, arguments, stacking and methods
lessons.summary: A decorator is a callable that takes a function and returns a replacement. This lesson covers preserving metadata, decorator factories, the order of stacked decorators, and what changes when the target is a method.

sections.heading: What @decorator means
Preserve metadata with functools.wraps
sections.body:
Without help, the decorated name is the `wrapper` function, so `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__qualname__` and `__module__` all describe `wrapper`. That breaks logging, `help()`, debugging and tools that introspect signatures.

`@functools.wraps(fn)` on the wrapper copies those attributes, updates `__dict__`, and sets `wrapper.__wrapped__ = fn` so the original can be reached (for example by `inspect.signature`).

sections.heading: Decorators with arguments
Stacking order
sections.body:
Stacked decorators are applied **bottom-up** (the one nearest `def` first):

```python
@a
@b
def g(): ...
# same as g = a(b(g))
```

At call time the outermost wrapper runs first, so `a`'s wrapper runs before `b`'s, which runs before `g`. Order matters for things like timing (does it include the auth check?) and caching (is the cache keyed before or after validation?).

sections.heading: Decorating methods
sections.body:
A function-based decorator works on methods because the wrapper is itself a plain function, and functions are non-data descriptors: looking the wrapper up on an instance binds it, so `self` arrives as the first positional argument in `*args`.

A **class-based** decorator (an object with `__call__`) is not a descriptor by default, so it is not bound. Calling `obj.method()` then fails with "missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'". Either implement `__get__` (for example returning `functools.partial(self.__call__, obj)`) or use a function-based decorator.

keyPoints: @d on def f is f = d(f), executed once at definition time.
Always use functools.wraps on wrappers; it also sets __wrapped__.
A decorator with arguments is a factory: retry(times) returns the real decorator.
Stacked decorators apply bottom-up; at call time the top wrapper runs first.
Function wrappers bind as methods; class-based decorators need __get__ to receive self.

gotchas.trap: The decorator body runs every time the function is called.
gotchas.correct: The decorator runs once when the def executes; only the wrapper it returns runs on each call.

gotchas.trap: With @a over @b, b's wrapper runs first when the function is called.
gotchas.correct: b is applied first, but a wraps the result, so a's wrapper runs first at call time.

lessons.lab: Write a timing decorator with and without functools.wraps and compare __name__, __doc__ and inspect.signature. Turn it into a factory that takes a label. Then write a class-based call counter, apply it to a method, observe the TypeError, and fix it with __get__.

lessons.title: Iterators, generators and yield from
lessons.summary: The iterator protocol behind every for loop, the difference between iterables and iterators, and how generators suspend, receive values, delegate and clean up.

sections.heading: The iterator protocol
sections.body:
An **iterable** has `__iter__` that returns an iterator (lists, dicts, strings, files). An **iterator** has `__next__`, which returns the next item or raises `StopIteration`, plus `__iter__` that returns **itself**.

A `for` loop calls `iter(obj)` once and then `next()` until `StopIteration`. Because `iter(it) is it` for an iterator, an iterator can be consumed only once:

```python
it = iter([1, 2, 3])
list(it), list(it)    # ([1, 2, 3], [])
```

A list can be looped over many times because each `iter(list)` makes a new iterator. `iter(callable, sentinel)` is a second form that calls the callable until it returns the sentinel.

sections.heading: Generators are iterators
sections.body:
A function containing `yield` returns a **generator** when called; its body does not run until the first `next()`. Each `yield` suspends the frame with all local state intact.

Generator objects and generator expressions are iterators, so they are single-use. Passing a generator to a function that loops over its argument twice silently gives an empty second pass. Materialise with `list()` when the data fits in memory, or restructure the work into one pass.

Since 3.7 (PEP 479), a `StopIteration` raised inside a generator body is converted to `RuntimeError`. To finish a generator, just `return`.

sections.heading: send, throw and close
sections.body:
PEP 342 made `yield` an expression:

- `gen.send(v)` resumes the generator and makes `v` the value of the paused `yield` expression. A new generator must be started with `next(gen)` or `gen.send(None)`; sending a non-None value to a just-started generator raises `TypeError`.
- `gen.throw(exc)` raises the exception at the paused `yield`. If the generator handles it and yields again, `throw` returns that value.
- `gen.close()` raises `GeneratorExit` at the paused `yield`, so `finally` blocks and `with` blocks inside the generator run. If the generator yields another value instead of exiting, `close()` raises `RuntimeError`.

```python
def averager():
    total = count = 0
    avg = None
    while True:
        x = yield avg
        total += x; count += 1
        avg = total / count
g = averager(); next(g)     # prime it
g.send(10)                  # 10.0
```

sections.heading: yield from delegates
sections.body:
PEP 380's `yield from sub` does more than loop and re-yield:

- It works with **any iterable**, yielding each item.
- For a subgenerator, it forwards `send()`, `throw()` and `close()` from the caller to the subgenerator.
- The value of the `yield from` expression is the subgenerator's **return value** (carried on `StopIteration.value`).

```python
def sub():
    x = yield 1
    return f"done {x}"
def outer():
    result = yield from sub()
    yield result
o = outer(); next(o)   # 1
o.send(5)              # 'done 5'
```

sections.heading: Deterministic cleanup
sections.body: A generator that is abandoned mid-iteration (say, the consumer `break`s) keeps its resources until it is closed. CPython's reference counting usually finalises it promptly, but that is an implementation detail. For deterministic release of files or connections, call `gen.close()` explicitly or use `contextlib.closing(gen)`.

keyPoints: Iterables return a new iterator from __iter__; iterators return themselves and are single-use.
Calling a generator function runs nothing until the first next().
Prime a generator with next() or send(None) before sending values.
close() raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield so finally and with blocks run.
The value of yield from is the subgenerator's return value, and send/throw/close are forwarded.

gotchas.trap: Calling iter() on a used generator rewinds it.
gotchas.correct: iter(gen) returns the same exhausted generator. Re-create it or keep the data in a list.

gotchas.trap: raise StopIteration is the way to end a generator early.
gotchas.correct: Since 3.7 it becomes RuntimeError (PEP 479). Use return.

gotchas.trap: Catching GeneratorExit and yielding a final value is a clean shutdown.
gotchas.correct: Yielding after GeneratorExit makes close() raise RuntimeError; let it propagate or just return.

lessons.lab: Implement a class-based iterator and an equivalent generator for a countdown. Build a priming decorator for coroutine-style generators, then write an outer generator that uses yield from and prints the subgenerator's return value. Wrap a file-reading generator in contextlib.closing and break out early to confirm the finally block runs.

lessons.title: Lazy pipelines with itertools and generator expressions
lessons.summary: Chaining generator expressions and itertools to process streams in constant memory, plus the places where laziness surprises you.

sections.heading: Why laziness
sections.body:
A list comprehension builds the whole result in memory. A generator expression produces one item at a time, so a chain of them processes a stream of any size in roughly constant memory:

```python
with open(path) as f:
    lines = (line.rstrip("\n") for line in f)
    errors = (l for l in lines if "ERROR" in l)
    count = sum(1 for _ in errors)
```

In Python 3, `map`, `filter`, `zip` and `enumerate` are lazy iterators too.

sections.heading: Useful itertools building blocks
sections.body:
- `islice(it, n)` takes a slice of any iterator, including infinite ones like `count()`.
- `chain(a, b)` and `chain.from_iterable(iterables)` flatten one level lazily.
- `accumulate` produces running totals; `pairwise` (3.10) yields overlapping pairs.
- `groupby(it, key)` groups **consecutive** items with equal keys. Unsorted input gives repeated groups (`"aabaa"` gives `a, b, a`), so sort by the same key first or use a dict.
- `batched(it, n)` (3.12) yields tuples of up to `n` items; the last batch may be shorter. In 3.13, `strict=True` raises `ValueError` on an incomplete final batch.
- `tee(it, n)` splits one iterator into several independent ones.

sections.heading: Where laziness bites
sections.body:
- **Single pass.** Every iterator in the pipeline is consumed once. Summing a generator twice gives the real sum and then 0.
- **Deferred errors and side effects.** Nothing runs until something consumes the pipeline, so exceptions surface at the consumer, possibly after the file has been closed.
- **Eager outermost iterable.** A generator expression evaluates its first `for` clause's iterable immediately; the rest is deferred.
- **tee buffers.** If one `tee` branch runs far ahead of another, the items in between are stored. If one branch will consume most of the data before the other starts, `list()` is simpler and faster.
- **zip truncates.** `zip` stops at the shortest input. The `zip(*[it]*n)` chunking idiom silently drops a partial tail; `strict=True` (3.10) raises on unequal lengths.

keyPoints: Generator expressions and itertools process streams in roughly constant memory.
groupby only groups consecutive equal keys; sort first.
batched (3.12) keeps the short final batch; strict=True (3.13) rejects it.
Pipelines are single-pass, and errors surface only when something consumes them.
tee stores the gap between branches; use list() if one branch consumes most data first.

gotchas.trap: zip(*[it]*100) is a safe way to chunk an iterator.
gotchas.correct: It drops the incomplete final chunk. Use itertools.batched (3.12+).

gotchas.trap: groupby returns one group per distinct key.
gotchas.correct: It returns one group per run of consecutive equal keys.

lessons.lab: Build a pipeline that streams a large generated log file, filters error lines, parses a field and counts by key, measuring peak memory with tracemalloc against a list-based version. Then show the groupby pitfall on unsorted data and chunk records with batched.

lessons.title: functools and first-class functions
lessons.summary: Functions are objects you can pass, store and return. functools builds on that with partial application, memoisation, type-based dispatch and folds.

sections.heading: First-class functions
sections.body: Functions are ordinary objects: they can be assigned, stored in dicts (dispatch tables), passed as `key=` arguments and returned from other functions. They carry attributes such as `__name__`, `__defaults__` and `__closure__`.

sections.heading: partial
sections.body:
`functools.partial(func, *args, **kwargs)` returns a callable with some arguments frozen. The frozen values are captured **when the partial is created**, which also makes it a clean fix for late binding in loops.

```python
parse_bin = functools.partial(int, base=2)
parse_bin("101")        # 5
parse_bin.func, parse_bin.keywords   # (int, {'base': 2})
```

sections.heading: lru_cache and cache
sections.body:
`@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)` memoises results keyed on the arguments; the bare `@lru_cache` form is allowed (3.8+) and the default `maxsize` is 128. `functools.cache` (3.9) is an unbounded cache. Decorated functions get `cache_info()` (hits, misses, maxsize, currsize) and `cache_clear()`.

- All arguments must be **hashable**: passing a list or dict raises `TypeError: unhashable type`.
- Only cache **pure** functions; a cached result is returned even if the outside world changed.
- On a method, `self` is part of the key and the cache holds references to instances, keeping them alive until they age out (or forever with `cache`). The Programming FAQ discusses alternatives such as `cached_property`.

sections.heading: singledispatch
sections.body: `@functools.singledispatch` turns a function into a generic function that dispatches on the **type of the first argument**. Register implementations with `@fn.register` and a type annotation, or `@fn.register(int)`. Dispatch follows the argument type's MRO, so a `bool` uses the `int` implementation unless `bool` is registered. For methods, use `functools.singledispatchmethod`, which dispatches on the first argument after `self`.

sections.heading: reduce
sections.body: `functools.reduce(func, iterable[, initial])` folds an iterable left to right. It lives in `functools` (it is not a builtin in Python 3). With an empty iterable and no initial value it raises `TypeError`, so pass an initial value when the input can be empty. For common folds, prefer `sum`, `math.prod`, `max`, `any` or `all`, which are clearer.

keyPoints: partial freezes arguments at creation time.
lru_cache defaults to maxsize 128; cache is unbounded; both need hashable arguments.
Caching a method keeps its instances alive through the cache.
singledispatch dispatches on the first argument's type via its MRO; singledispatchmethod skips self.
reduce needs an initial value for possibly empty input.

gotchas.trap: Raising maxsize fixes TypeError: unhashable type from lru_cache.
gotchas.correct: The cache key must be hashable. Convert arguments to tuples or frozensets, or do not cache that function.

gotchas.trap: reduce over an empty list returns None.
gotchas.correct: It raises TypeError unless an initial value is given.

lessons.lab: Memoise a recursive Fibonacci with lru_cache and read cache_info(). Write a singledispatch serializer for int, list and dict and check which implementation bool uses. Replace a lambda-in-a-loop bug with partial.

lessons.title: Names, references and copying
lessons.summary: Python names are references to objects. Knowing when you rebind a name and when you mutate a shared object explains aliasing bugs, argument passing and the difference between shallow and deep copies.

sections.heading: Names are bound to objects
sections.body:
An assignment such as `b = a` never copies anything. It binds the name `b` to the same object `a` already refers to. Both names are now **aliases**, so `b is a` is `True`.

Whether aliasing matters depends on mutability:

- **Immutable objects** (int, str, tuple, frozenset) cannot change, so sharing them is harmless. Any "change" produces a new object and rebinds the name.
- **Mutable objects** (list, dict, set, most user classes) can be changed in place, and every alias sees the change.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)   # [1, 2, 3]: same list
b = [9]    # rebinding b; a is untouched
```

sections.heading: Mutation versus rebinding
sections.body:
Two operations look alike but are very different:

- **Rebinding** (`x = ...`) points a name at a different object. Other aliases keep the old object.
- **Mutation** (`x.append(...)`, `x[k] = v`, `x.update(...)`) changes the object itself, so all aliases see it.

Augmented assignment sits in between. For a list, `x += [4]` calls `list.__iadd__`, which mutates in place and then rebinds `x` to the same object. For a tuple or int, `+=` builds a new object and rebinds only that name.

The classic trap combines both: `t = ([1],); t[0] += [2]` mutates the inner list **and then** raises `TypeError` when it tries to store the result back into the tuple. The Programming FAQ explains this case.

sections.heading: Argument passing is by assignment
sections.body:
Calling `f(obj)` binds the parameter name to the caller's object, exactly like an assignment. The FAQ calls this passing arguments "by assignment". It is neither copy-by-value nor C++-style references.

- If the function **mutates** the parameter (`items.append(x)`), the caller sees the change.
- If the function **rebinds** the parameter (`items = items + [x]`), only the local name changes and the caller sees nothing.

To give results back, return them, rather than relying on mutation of arguments the caller may not expect to change.

sections.heading: Shallow and deep copies
sections.body:
The `copy` module offers two levels:

- `copy.copy(x)` makes a **shallow** copy: a new outer container whose elements are the same objects. `list(a)`, `a[:]`, `dict(d)` and `d.copy()` are also shallow.
- `copy.deepcopy(x)` copies recursively. It keeps a `memo` dict of objects already copied, so shared sub-objects stay shared in the copy and reference cycles do not loop forever.

Classes can customise this with `__copy__` and `__deepcopy__(memo)`. Functions and classes are "copied" by returning the original object unchanged, and types such as modules, frames, files and sockets are not copied at all.

**New in 3.13:** `copy.replace(obj, **changes)` creates a modified copy of objects that support `__replace__`, including dataclasses and named tuples. It is the generic form of `dataclasses.replace` and `namedtuple._replace`.

sections.heading: Common aliasing traps
sections.body:
- `grid = [[0] * 3] * 3` creates **one** inner list referenced three times. Setting `grid[0][0] = 1` changes every row. Use `[[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`.
- `dict.fromkeys(keys, [])` gives every key the same list. Use a comprehension or `collections.defaultdict(list)`.
- Shallow-copying a nested config template and then editing a nested value edits the template too. Use `deepcopy` or build fresh nested objects.
- Mutable default arguments are another form of the same sharing problem (covered with scopes in the functions domain).

keyPoints: Assignment binds a name; it never copies.
Mutation is visible through every alias; rebinding affects only that name.
Arguments are passed by assignment: functions can mutate but not rebind the caller's objects.
copy.copy is shallow; copy.deepcopy is recursive and uses a memo for shared objects and cycles.
copy.replace() is new in 3.13 for objects with __replace__.

gotchas.trap: `b = a` gives me an independent list.
gotchas.correct: It gives a second name for the same list. Use `a.copy()`, `list(a)` or `a[:]` for a shallow copy.

gotchas.trap: A shallow copy of a nested dict protects the original.
gotchas.correct: Only the outer dict is new. Nested dicts and lists are still shared; use `copy.deepcopy`.

gotchas.trap: `t[0] += [x]` on a tuple holding a list either works or does nothing.
gotchas.correct: The list is mutated and then `TypeError` is raised because the tuple item cannot be reassigned.

lessons.lab: In a REPL, build `grid = [[0]*3]*3`, set `grid[0][0] = 1` and print it. Then rebuild it with a comprehension. Next, make a nested dict, take `copy.copy` and `copy.deepcopy` of it, mutate a nested value in each copy, and use `is` to check which inner objects are shared.

lessons.title: Memory management in CPython
lessons.summary: CPython frees most objects through reference counting and uses a generational cyclic garbage collector for reference cycles. Weak references, careful finalisation and tracemalloc help you avoid and find leaks.

sections.heading: Reference counting
sections.body:
Every CPython object carries a reference count. When it drops to zero the object is freed **immediately**, which is why a file opened and dropped in CPython is usually closed right away.

`sys.getrefcount(obj)` reports the count, but it is always one higher than you expect because the call's own argument is a temporary reference.

Reference counting is a CPython implementation detail. Other implementations (and the language reference) do not promise prompt destruction, so portable code uses `with` blocks to release resources.

sections.heading: The cyclic garbage collector
sections.body:
Reference counting cannot free a **cycle**: two objects that refer to each other keep each other's counts above zero even when nothing else can reach them. The `gc` module's collector finds and frees such unreachable cycles.

- It is **generational** with three generations. New container objects start in the youngest generation; survivors are promoted, and older generations are scanned less often.
- `gc.collect()` forces a full collection and returns the number of collected plus uncollectable objects.
- `gc.disable()` turns off only the **cyclic** collector. Reference counting keeps working, so acyclic garbage is still freed, but cycles accumulate.
- `gc.freeze()` (3.7+) moves all current objects into a permanent generation that future collections ignore. Fork-based servers call it before forking to avoid copy-on-write page faults caused by the collector touching shared objects.
- `gc.get_referrers()` and `gc.get_referents()` help debug who is holding an object.

Do not depend on exact default thresholds; they are not documented as stable and have changed between versions.

sections.heading: Weak references
sections.body:
A **weak reference** refers to an object without increasing its reference count, so it does not keep the object alive. `weakref.ref(obj)()` returns the object, or `None` once it has been collected.

- `WeakValueDictionary` and `WeakKeyDictionary` make caches and registries that do not cause leaks.
- `WeakSet` tracks a set of live objects, such as observers.
- Not every object supports weak references. Built-in `int`, `str`, `tuple`, `list` and `dict` instances do not (subclasses of `list` and `dict` do). A class that defines `__slots__` must include `'__weakref__'` to be weakly referenceable.

sections.heading: Finalizers and __del__ pitfalls
sections.body:
`__del__` runs when an object is about to be destroyed, but it is a poor cleanup tool:

- Its timing is not guaranteed, and it may not run at all for objects still alive at interpreter exit.
- Exceptions raised inside it are ignored, with only a warning printed to `sys.stderr`.
- It can accidentally resurrect the object by storing `self` somewhere.

Since Python 3.4 (PEP 442), objects with `__del__` that are part of cycles are collected normally instead of being parked in `gc.garbage`.

Prefer **context managers** for deterministic cleanup, and `weakref.finalize(obj, func, *args)` for a safety-net callback. Make sure `func` and `args` do not reference `obj`, or the finalizer keeps it alive.

sections.heading: Finding leaks with tracemalloc
sections.body:
`tracemalloc` records where Python memory blocks were allocated.

```python
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
run_suspect_workload()
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for stat in after.compare_to(before, 'lineno')[:10]:
    print(stat)
```

- Start tracing **early**; allocations made before `start()` are not tracked.
- `start(nframe)` stores more traceback frames per allocation at higher overhead.
- Compare snapshots taken across repeated iterations of the workload. Steady growth at one line points to the leak, often an ever-growing cache or global list.

keyPoints: Refcount zero frees an object immediately in CPython; this is an implementation detail.
The cyclic GC is generational (three generations) and only handles cycles.
gc.disable() leaves reference counting on; only cycles leak.
Weak references and WeakValueDictionary build caches that do not keep objects alive.
Prefer with blocks and weakref.finalize over __del__.
tracemalloc snapshot compare_to finds the lines whose allocations grow.

gotchas.trap: `gc.disable()` turns off all memory freeing.
gotchas.correct: Only the cyclic collector stops. Reference counting still frees acyclic objects.

gotchas.trap: Objects with `__del__` in a cycle always leak into `gc.garbage`.
gotchas.correct: That was true before 3.4. Since PEP 442 they are collected normally.

gotchas.trap: A `weakref.finalize` callback can safely be a bound method of the object.
gotchas.correct: A bound method references the object and keeps it alive, so the finalizer never fires on collection.

lessons.lab: Create two objects that reference each other, take a weakref to one, delete the names and check the weakref (still alive). Call `gc.collect()` and check again. Then use tracemalloc to snapshot before and after appending 100,000 strings to a global list and print the top three `compare_to` lines.

lessons.title: How CPython runs your code
lessons.summary: Source is compiled to code objects holding bytecode, which the interpreter executes inside frames. The dis module lets you read bytecode, but the instructions are a version-specific implementation detail.

sections.heading: From source to code objects
sections.body:
CPython compiles each module, class body and function body into a **code object**. A code object is immutable and holds the bytecode plus metadata such as constants (`co_consts`), local variable names (`co_varnames`) and the filename and line table.

- `func.__code__` is the code object of a function. Every call of the function reuses the same code object.
- The built-in `compile()` turns source text into a code object that `exec()` or `eval()` can run.
- When a module is **imported**, the compiled bytecode is cached as a `.pyc` file in `__pycache__`, named with an interpreter tag such as `cpython-313`. The script you run directly as `python script.py` is compiled but not cached.

sections.heading: Frames
sections.body:
Each call creates a **frame**: the runtime state of one execution of a code object. A frame holds the local variables, the current instruction position and a link to the calling frame.

- Two simultaneous calls of the same function share one code object but have separate frames, which is why recursion and threads each get their own locals.
- Tracebacks are built from frames, and `inspect.currentframe()` or `sys._getframe()` expose them for debugging. Keeping a frame reference keeps all its locals alive, so delete such references when done.

sections.heading: Reading bytecode with dis
sections.body:
`dis.dis(func)` disassembles a function into human-readable instructions such as loads, stores, calls and binary operations.

Use it conceptually, for example to see that `x += 1` is several separate instructions (load, add, store), or that a generator expression compiles to its own nested code object. Do not write tests or tools that depend on exact opcodes: the `dis` docs state that bytecode is an implementation detail and carries no guarantee of staying the same between Python versions.

sections.heading: The specializing adaptive interpreter
sections.body:
Since 3.11, CPython uses a **specializing adaptive interpreter** (PEP 659). As code runs, generic instructions are replaced by specialised forms tuned for the types actually observed, such as an attribute load for a particular class layout. If assumptions stop holding, the instruction falls back to the generic path.

Specialisation never changes semantics. `dis.dis(func, adaptive=True)` shows the specialised instructions after the function has warmed up.

**Newer versions:** 3.13 adds an experimental JIT that is off by default. Treat it as opt-in and experimental in 3.13.

keyPoints: Code objects are immutable bytecode plus metadata; func.__code__ is shared across calls.
Frames hold per-call state: locals, position and the caller link.
Imported modules get cached .pyc files in __pycache__; the main script does not.
dis is for understanding; bytecode is version-specific.
3.11+ specializes instructions adaptively without changing behaviour.

gotchas.trap: A test can assert on the opcodes `dis` prints.
gotchas.correct: Bytecode changes between versions; assert on behaviour, not instructions.

gotchas.trap: Each call compiles the function again.
gotchas.correct: The function's code object is compiled once and reused; each call gets a new frame.

lessons.lab: Write a function that does `total += x` in a loop and run `dis.dis` on it. Find the load, add and store steps. Call it a few thousand times, then run `dis.dis(f, adaptive=True)` and look for specialised instruction names.

lessons.title: The GIL and free-threaded Python
lessons.summary: On the default build the global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. It does not make your compound operations atomic, and Python 3.13 adds an experimental free-threaded build without it.

sections.heading: What the GIL does
sections.body:
In the default CPython build, the **global interpreter lock** ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. It protects the interpreter's own internals, such as reference counts.

Consequences:

- Threads still help **I/O-bound** work, because blocking I/O and many C extensions release the GIL while they wait.
- Threads do **not** speed up **CPU-bound pure Python**. Use `ProcessPoolExecutor` or `multiprocessing` on GIL builds.

sections.heading: What it does not protect
sections.body:
The GIL makes individual bytecode steps effectively atomic; some single operations on built-ins, such as `list.append`, are atomic in CPython as a result (see the Library FAQ). But a thread switch can happen **between** steps.

`counter += 1` is a load, an add and a store. Two threads can both load the same value and one increment is lost. The same goes for check-then-act code such as `if key not in d: d[key] = make()`.

Protect shared mutable state with `threading.Lock` (or use `queue.Queue`). Code that is correct only because of the GIL is fragile, and it breaks outright on a free-threaded build.

sections.heading: The free-threaded build in 3.13
sections.body:
PEP 703 makes the GIL optional. In 3.13 this is an **experimental, separate build**, typically installed as `python3.13t`. It is not the default interpreter.

- Check the build with `sysconfig.get_config_var('Py_GIL_DISABLED')` and the runtime state with `sys._is_gil_enabled()` (new in 3.13).
- The `PYTHON_GIL` environment variable and the `-X gil` option force the GIL off or on in that build.
- Importing a C extension that is not marked as free-thread-safe **re-enables the GIL** for the process (with a warning), unless you force it off.
- The 3.13 docs warn of a substantial single-threaded performance cost in the experimental build.

To make this safe without a GIL, PEP 703 changes reference counting (biased reference counting, immortal and deferred objects) and adds per-object locking inside built-in containers.

sections.heading: Newer versions
sections.body: In 3.14, PEP 779 moved the free-threaded build to **officially supported** (no longer experimental), but it is still a separate build rather than the default. When you write about 3.13, call it experimental.

keyPoints: The GIL lets one thread run bytecode at a time on default builds.
Threads help I/O-bound work; processes help CPU-bound pure Python on GIL builds.
x += 1 is not atomic; use a Lock for shared mutable state.
3.13 free-threading is an experimental separate build (python3.13t).
sys._is_gil_enabled() reports whether the GIL is active at runtime.
Unmarked C extensions re-enable the GIL in the free-threaded build.

gotchas.trap: Because of the GIL I never need locks.
gotchas.correct: The GIL does not make compound operations atomic. Read-modify-write and check-then-act need a lock.

gotchas.trap: Installing 3.13 removes the GIL.
gotchas.correct: The default 3.13 build has the GIL. Free-threading is a separate, experimental build.

lessons.lab: Run four threads that each do `counter += 1` a million times on a shared global and print the final value (it may come up short). Add a `threading.Lock` around the increment and run again. Then print `sys._is_gil_enabled()` to confirm which build you are on.
