rationales: Without a GIL races are at least as likely; locking is still needed.
Correct: a lock makes the read-modify-write exclusive.
The GIL does not make compound operations atomic.
Changing the switch interval makes races rarer, not impossible.

sources.title: Library and Extension FAQ — Python 3.13 docs

questions.scenario: A data team parallelises a pure-Python numeric loop with `ThreadPoolExecutor(8)` on the default 3.13 build and sees no speedup over one thread.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Add `threading.Lock` around the loop body
Increase the pool to 64 threads
Use `asyncio.gather` over the loop iterations
Use `ProcessPoolExecutor` so work runs in separate processes
questions.explanation: On a GIL build only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound pure Python does not scale with threads. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL.
rationales: A lock serialises the work further.
More threads still contend for one GIL and add overhead.
asyncio is single-threaded cooperative concurrency; it does not add CPU parallelism.
Correct: processes sidestep the GIL for CPU-bound work.

questions.scenario: You run a CPU-bound threaded workload on `python3.13t` expecting parallel speedup, but it behaves like the GIL build. A warning appeared at startup when a third-party C extension was imported.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and how do you confirm it?
options: The free-threaded build only removes the GIL for asyncio tasks; check `asyncio.get_event_loop()`
`python3.13t` always runs with the GIL unless compiled with the JIT; check `sys.flags.optimize`
Threads must be created with `daemon=True` to run in parallel; check `threading.enumerate()`
The extension is not marked free-thread-safe, so the GIL was re-enabled; check `sys._is_gil_enabled()`
questions.explanation: In the free-threaded build, importing a C extension that does not declare free-threading support re-enables the GIL for the process unless it is forced off with `PYTHON_GIL=0` or `-X gil=0`. `sys._is_gil_enabled()` (3.13+) reports the runtime state.
rationales: Free-threading applies to threads, not specifically asyncio.
The JIT is unrelated to the GIL.
Daemon status does not affect parallelism.
Correct: unmarked extensions re-enable the GIL.

questions.scenario: A team is evaluating Python 3.13's free-threaded build for a service.
questions.stem: Which statements are accurate for 3.13? (Select two.)
options: It is the default interpreter installed by 3.13
It removes the need for locks around shared mutable state
It is an experimental build, separate from the default interpreter (a distinct executable such as `python3.13t`)
The `PYTHON_GIL` environment variable or `-X gil` option can force the GIL on or off in that build
questions.explanation: PEP 703 free-threading is experimental in 3.13 and ships as a separate build such as `python3.13t`. Without a GIL, data races in your own code are still possible, so locks remain necessary.
rationales: The default 3.13 build still has the GIL.
Removing the GIL makes correct locking more important, not less.
Correct: experimental, separate build in 3.13.
Correct: these controls are documented in the free-threading HOWTO.

questions.scenario: `orders.py` does `from customers import Customer` at top level and `customers.py` does `from orders import Order` at top level. Running `python -c 'import orders'` fails with an ImportError saying `Order` cannot be imported from `orders`.
questions.stem: Which changes resolve the error? (Select two.)
options: Call `importlib.reload(orders)` at the end of `customers.py`
Move the shared types into a third module that both import
In `customers.py`, use `import orders` and refer to `orders.Order` only inside functions at call time
Delete `customers` from `sys.modules` at the top of `orders.py`
questions.explanation: A module is placed in `sys.modules` before its body finishes, so the second import sees `orders` half-initialised and `Order` does not exist yet. Breaking the cycle or deferring the attribute lookup to call time avoids touching the missing name during import.
rationales: Reloading re-runs the module while still mid-import and does not fix the missing name.
Correct: removes the cycle.
Correct: binds the module object and looks up `Order` later, when it exists.
Removing cache entries causes double execution and new errors.

questions.scenario: A script in `~/tools/` starts with `import random` and fails with `AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'choice'`. The folder also contains a file the developer wrote called `random.py`.
questions.stem: What is happening?
options: The script's directory is first on `sys.path`, so the local `random.py` shadows the standard library module
The stdlib `random` module was removed in 3.13
`random` must be imported with `importlib.import_module`
A stale `.pyc` of the stdlib is being used
questions.explanation: When running a script, its directory is prepended to `sys.path`, so local modules are found before the standard library. Rename the local file (and remove its `__pycache__` entry), or use `-P`/`PYTHONSAFEPATH` to avoid prepending the directory.
rationales: Correct: local file shadows the stdlib.
`random` is still in the standard library.
The import mechanism and search order are the same either way.
The error comes from finding the wrong module, not a stale cache.

questions.scenario: In `proj/app/cli.py`, the line `from .util import parse` fails with "attempted relative import with no known parent package" when run as `python app/cli.py` from `proj/`.
questions.stem: What is the correct way to run it?
options: Rename `cli.py` to `__init__.py`
`python -m app.cli` from `proj/`
`cd app && python cli.py`
Add `app/` to `PYTHONPATH` and run `python app/cli.py`
questions.explanation: Running a file by path makes it `__main__` with no parent package, so relative imports cannot be resolved. `-m` imports it as `app.cli`, setting its package while still running it as `__main__`.
rationales: That changes the package structure rather than running the module correctly.
Correct: `-m` gives the module its package.
Running from inside the folder still has no parent package.
Changing the path does not give a directly run file a package.

questions.scenario: During a REPL session you edit `pricing.py` and call `importlib.reload(pricing)`. Code that earlier did `from pricing import rate` still uses the old behaviour, while `pricing.rate(...)` uses the new one.
questions.stem: Why?
options: `reload` creates a second module object and leaves the original in `sys.modules`
The new function is not visible until `gc.collect()` runs
`reload` re-executes the module in the same module object, but names already bound with `from ... import` still point to the old function
`reload` only works on packages, not modules
questions.explanation: `importlib.reload` re-runs the module's code in the existing module namespace, rebinding its globals. Other namespaces that copied a reference with `from pricing import rate` keep the previous function object.
rationales: The same module object is reused.
Garbage collection does not affect name bindings.
Correct: copied names are not updated.
Reload works on modules.

questions.scenario: A script on macOS creates a `multiprocessing.Pool` at module level, without any guard. It fails with errors about starting a new process before the current one has finished bootstrapping.
questions.stem: What fixes it?
options: Call `multiprocessing.freeze_support()` at the top of the module
Call `gc.freeze()` before creating the pool
Add the script directory to `sys.path`
Put the pool creation under `if __name__ == "__main__":`
questions.explanation: With the spawn start method (the default on macOS and Windows), each child imports the main module. Unguarded module-level code would try to create processes again, so it must be guarded by the `__main__` check.
rationales: `freeze_support()` is only for frozen Windows executables and has no effect on macOS; it does not stop the main module being re-run in children.
Freezing the GC is unrelated to process start.
The main module is found already; the problem is re-execution.
Correct: the guard prevents children re-running startup code.

questions.scenario: You want to load configuration modules from an encrypted archive by installing a custom importer.
questions.stem: Which design matches the import protocol?
options: Add the archive path to `sys.path` and rely on the default finder to decrypt it
Monkeypatch `builtins.open` so `import` reads decrypted files
Insert decrypted source strings into `sys.modules` as values
Add a finder to `sys.meta_path` whose `find_spec()` returns a `ModuleSpec` with a loader that implements `exec_module()`
questions.explanation: Imports consult finders on `sys.meta_path`, each of which may return a `ModuleSpec`. The spec's loader creates the module and runs its code with `exec_module()`, so a custom finder and loader pair is the supported extension point.
rationales: The default path finder cannot decrypt archives.
Import does not go through `builtins.open`, and patching it is fragile.
`sys.modules` must map names to module objects, not source strings.
Correct: the documented finder/loader protocol.

questions.scenario: A team's report generator spends 95% of its time in a pure-Python scoring loop over large in-memory lists. It runs on standard CPython 3.13 on an 8-core machine.
questions.stem: Which change is most likely to cut wall-clock time?
options: Run chunks in a ThreadPoolExecutor with 8 workers
Rewrite the loop as asyncio tasks with gather
Run chunks in a ProcessPoolExecutor
Wrap each chunk in asyncio.to_thread
questions.explanation: The work is CPU-bound pure Python, and on the default GIL build only one thread runs bytecode at a time. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so they can use multiple cores.
rationales: Threads contend for the GIL on CPU-bound pure Python, so throughput barely changes.
asyncio is single-threaded and only overlaps waiting, not computation.
Correct: processes run in parallel on separate cores.
to_thread uses threads, which share the GIL, so CPU-bound work is not parallelised.

questions.scenario: A script must download 300 files from an internal server using a blocking HTTP library that has no async version. The download count is fixed and modest.
questions.stem: What is the simplest effective approach?
options: A ProcessPoolExecutor with one process per file
A ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded number of workers
Calling the library directly inside async def functions run with gather
A single thread, since the GIL prevents I/O concurrency anyway
questions.explanation: The work is I/O-bound, and blocking I/O releases the GIL, so a pool of threads overlaps the waits while still using the blocking library. Processes add pickling and start-up cost for no benefit here.
rationales: Processes work but add unnecessary overhead for I/O-bound work.
Correct: threads overlap blocking I/O and work with ordinary libraries.
A blocking call inside a coroutine blocks the loop, so the downloads still run one at a time.
Wrong: threads waiting on I/O release the GIL and do run concurrently.

questions.stem: A developer submits 10 jobs to a ThreadPoolExecutor and wants to log each result the moment it finishes, whichever finishes first. Which call fits?
options: executor.map(job, inputs)
concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures)
[f.result() for f in futures]
executor.shutdown(wait=False)
questions.explanation: as_completed yields futures in the order they complete. Executor.map and a list comprehension over futures both return results in submission order, blocking on slower earlier items.
rationales: map returns results in input order, so a slow first job delays every log line.
Correct: futures are yielded as they finish.
This waits on each future in submission order.
shutdown does not return results; wait=False just stops waiting for pending work.

questions.scenario: On macOS, this module runs at import time: `pool = ProcessPoolExecutor(); print(list(pool.map(lambda x: x * 2, range(10))))`. It fails.
questions.stem: Which two changes are needed for it to work reliably? (Select two.)
options: Replace the lambda with a module-level function
Switch to ThreadPoolExecutor to get true parallelism
Move pool creation and use under if __name__ == "__main__":
Increase max_workers so the lambda fits in each worker
questions.explanation: Work sent to a process pool must be picklable, and lambdas are not. macOS uses the spawn start method, so each worker imports the main module, and unguarded top-level pool code would run again in every worker.
rationales: Correct: module-level functions are picklable by reference.
Threads would not give CPU parallelism on a GIL build and do not address the stated failure.
Correct: the guard stops workers from re-executing the pool code on import.
Worker count has nothing to do with picklability.

questions.scenario:
```python
async def main():
    a = await fetch(1)
    b = await fetch(2)
    c = await fetch(3)
```
Each fetch awaits a 1-second network call.
questions.stem: About how long does main() take, and why?
options: About 1 second, because await runs coroutines concurrently
About 3 seconds, because each await finishes before the next starts
About 1 second, because asyncio.run uses a thread per await
It never finishes, because fetch is never scheduled
questions.explanation: Awaiting a coroutine runs it to completion before the next line runs, so consecutive awaits are sequential. To overlap them, wrap them in tasks or a TaskGroup.
rationales: await alone does not create concurrency.
Correct: the calls run one after another.
asyncio runs tasks on one thread; there is no thread per await.
Awaiting a coroutine does run it.

questions.scenario: A web handler starts an audit write with `asyncio.create_task(write_audit(event))` and returns without keeping the result. Occasionally audit rows go missing, with no errors in the logs.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The loop only holds weak references to tasks; store tasks in a set and discard them in a done callback
create_task runs in a new thread that is killed at exit; use asyncio.to_thread instead
write_audit was never awaited; add await in front of create_task
Tasks are limited to 100 per loop; raise the limit
questions.explanation: The asyncio docs warn that the event loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so a task with no other reference can disappear mid-execution. Keeping a strong reference in a collection and removing it when done is the documented pattern.
rationales: Correct: this is the documented fire-and-forget pitfall and fix.
Tasks run on the event loop thread, not a new thread.
create_task does schedule the coroutine; awaiting it would make the handler wait, which defeats the purpose.
There is no such task limit.

questions.scenario: Three coroutines are run with `await asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c())`. a() raises ValueError after 1 second; b() and c() would take 10 seconds and write to a database.
questions.stem: What happens to b() and c()?
options: They are cancelled immediately when a() fails
They keep running; the ValueError propagates to the awaiter of gather
gather waits for all three, then raises an ExceptionGroup
They are paused until the exception is handled
questions.explanation: With return_exceptions=False, gather propagates the first exception, but the docs state the other awaitables are not cancelled and continue to run. TaskGroup is the API that cancels siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup.
rationales: That is TaskGroup's behaviour, not gather's.
Correct: siblings keep running in the background.
That describes TaskGroup.
asyncio has no such pause mechanism.

questions.scenario: A service fetches a user's profile, orders and preferences concurrently. If any fetch fails, the others should be cancelled and no fetch should outlive the request handler.
questions.stem: Which construct best fits?
options: asyncio.gather with return_exceptions=True
asyncio.TaskGroup
Three asyncio.create_task calls with no await
asyncio.wait with return_when=ALL_COMPLETED
questions.explanation: TaskGroup cancels the remaining tasks when one fails and the async with block does not exit until every child has finished. That gives the structured, no-orphan behaviour required.
rationales: This collects errors but cancels nothing.
Correct: failure cancels siblings and the block bounds their lifetime.
Unawaited tasks can outlive the handler and errors go unnoticed.
ALL_COMPLETED waits for everything and does not cancel on failure.

questions.stem: A batch job runs 200 validations concurrently and must report every result, including which ones raised, without stopping early. Which call fits best?
options: asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(*coros), None)
async with asyncio.TaskGroup() and a bare except Exception
asyncio.gather(*coros)
asyncio.gather(*coros, return_exceptions=True)
questions.explanation: With return_exceptions=True, gather treats exceptions like successful results and places them in the result list in order. TaskGroup and plain gather both stop at the first failure from the caller's view.
rationales: wait_for adds a timeout (none here) and does not change error handling.
TaskGroup cancels the rest on the first failure.
The first exception propagates and the other results are lost to the caller.
Correct: every result or exception is returned in order.

questions.stem: What is wrong?
options: BaseException includes CancelledError, so the cancellation is swallowed and the task never exits
log.exception cannot be called inside a coroutine
TaskGroup does not support while loops
process must be wrapped in asyncio.shield
questions.explanation: Cancellation is delivered as CancelledError, a BaseException subclass. Catching it without re-raising keeps the task alive, and the docs warn that swallowing it breaks TaskGroup and timeout. Catch Exception, or re-raise CancelledError.
rationales: Correct: the cancellation request is swallowed.
Logging is fine in coroutines.
There is no such restriction.
shield would make cancellation harder, not easier.

questions.stem: In Python 3.13, which code correctly falls back to None when a call takes longer than 5 seconds?
options:
```python
async with asyncio.timeout(5):
    try:
        r = await call()
    except TimeoutError:
        r = None
```

```python
try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(5):
        r = await call()
except TimeoutError:
    r = None
```

```python
try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(5):
        r = await call()
except asyncio.CancelledError:
    r = None
```

```python
r = await asyncio.timeout(5, call())
```
questions.explanation: asyncio.timeout cancels the task and converts the CancelledError into TimeoutError as it exits the block, so the docs say it can only be caught outside. Since 3.11, asyncio.TimeoutError is the built-in TimeoutError.
rationales: Inside the block the task sees CancelledError, not TimeoutError.
Correct: catch TimeoutError outside the async with.
The CancelledError is converted on exit, so it is not what escapes.
asyncio.timeout is a context manager, not a wrapper call.

questions.scenario: A payment-capture coroutine must finish once started, even if the request that triggered it is cancelled by a client disconnect.
questions.stem: Which approach matches that requirement?
options: await capture() inside an asyncio.timeout(None) block
await asyncio.wait_for(capture(), None)
Catch CancelledError in the handler and call capture() again
await asyncio.shield(capture()) inside the handler
questions.explanation: shield protects the inner awaitable from cancellation of the awaiting task: the handler is cancelled but capture keeps running. The other options either run it normally (so it is cancelled with the handler) or restart it. The docs also advise keeping a reference to the task passed to shield so it cannot be garbage-collected mid-execution.
rationales: timeout(None) sets no deadline but does not block cancellation.
No timeout, but cancellation still propagates into capture.
Retrying risks a double capture and the original is still cancelled.
Correct: the inner awaitable is protected from the outer cancellation.

questions.scenario: Code inside a TaskGroup raises ValueError in one task and ConnectionError in another. The handler is `except ValueError: ...`.
questions.stem: What happens?
options: The ValueError handler runs and the ConnectionError is ignored
Only the first exception raised is delivered, so the handler may run
The ExceptionGroup is not matched by except ValueError and propagates
Python raises a SyntaxError because except* is required after TaskGroup
questions.explanation: TaskGroup raises an ExceptionGroup, which is not itself a ValueError, so a plain except clause does not match it. except* ValueError would match the subgroup.
rationales: A plain except does not look inside groups.
TaskGroup combines failures into one group.
Correct: the group propagates unhandled.
Plain except is valid syntax; it just does not match.

questions.stem: What is the outcome? (Select two.)
options: "V" is printed
Only the first matching clause runs, so "K" is not printed
"K" is printed
Nothing escapes the try statement
questions.explanation: Each except* clause receives the subgroup of exceptions it matches, and several clauses can run for one group. The unmatched TypeError is re-raised in an ExceptionGroup, so something does escape.
rationales: Correct: the ValueError subgroup is handled.
Unlike except, multiple except* clauses can run.
Correct: the KeyError subgroup is handled.
TypeError matches no clause and is re-raised.

questions.stem: Which statement about except* is accurate?
options: It can be combined with plain except clauses in the same try
A return statement is allowed inside an except* clause
It can match exceptions inside an ExceptionGroup by type
It only works in async functions
questions.explanation: PEP 654 introduces except* to match subgroups of an exception group by type. It cannot be mixed with except in the same try, and break, continue and return are not allowed in its clauses.
rationales: Mixing except and except* is a syntax error.
return, break and continue are disallowed in except* clauses.
Correct: that is its purpose.
except* works in ordinary synchronous code too.

questions.scenario: An async API server's p99 latency spikes to 2 seconds for every endpoint whenever the /report endpoint is hit. /report calls `requests.get()` on an upstream service inside its async handler.
questions.stem: What is the root cause?
options: The upstream service is slow, which only affects /report
A blocking call in a coroutine stalls the event loop for all tasks
The server needs more event loops per thread
requests.get raises CancelledError that propagates to other handlers
questions.explanation: The event loop runs in one thread, and a blocking call holds it until it returns, so every other task waits too. The fix is an async client or await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url).
rationales: If the call did not block, only /report would be slow.
Correct: the blocking call freezes the whole loop.
One loop per thread is the model; more loops does not fix blocking calls in handlers.
A blocking call does not raise CancelledError into other tasks.

questions.scenario: An async service needs to (1) call a legacy blocking file-upload SDK and (2) run a heavy pure-Python PDF layout step, without stalling the event loop and using multiple cores for step 2.
questions.stem: Which combination fits best?
options: asyncio.to_thread for both
asyncio.to_thread for the upload; loop.run_in_executor with a ProcessPoolExecutor for the layout
A ProcessPoolExecutor for the upload; asyncio.to_thread for the layout
Call both directly; asyncio parallelises them automatically
questions.explanation: to_thread moves blocking I/O off the loop, but the docs note it does not speed up CPU-bound pure Python under the GIL. A process pool via run_in_executor gives true parallelism for the layout.
rationales: The layout step would still be limited by the GIL.
Correct: threads for blocking I/O, processes for CPU-bound work.
This reverses the fit; the upload does not need a process and the layout does.
Direct blocking calls stall the loop; asyncio does not parallelise them.

questions.scenario: A notification helper is written `async def notify(user): ...`. A developer calls `notify(user)` from another coroutine without await. Tests pass, but no notifications are sent.
questions.stem: Which two signals point to the bug? (Select two.)
options: A RuntimeWarning that the coroutine was never awaited
A CancelledError traceback in the logs
With asyncio debug mode on, a traceback showing where the coroutine was created
A TimeoutError from the event loop
questions.explanation: Calling a coroutine function only creates a coroutine object; if it is never awaited, Python emits a 'never awaited' RuntimeWarning. Debug mode adds the traceback of where it was created.
rationales: Correct: this is the standard warning for an un-awaited coroutine.
Nothing was scheduled, so nothing was cancelled.
Correct: debug mode reports the creation point.
Nothing ran, so no timeout fires.

questions.scenario: A crawler does `await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))` over 40 000 URLs. It soon fails with 'too many open files' and the target site starts rate-limiting.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Wrap each fetch in async with on a shared asyncio.Semaphore(50)
Replace gather with a TaskGroup, which limits concurrency automatically
Use asyncio.to_thread for each fetch
Add await asyncio.sleep(0) before each fetch
questions.explanation: A semaphore caps how many fetches are in flight at once, bounding sockets and request rate. TaskGroup changes error handling, not concurrency, and sleep(0) only yields without limiting anything.
rationales: Correct: at most 50 fetches run at a time.
TaskGroup does not limit the number of concurrent tasks.
Threads still start all 40 000 fetches, now with thread overhead.
Yielding once does not cap concurrency.

questions.scenario: Eight threads each run `for _ in range(100_000): stats['hits'] += 1` on a shared dict in standard CPython 3.13. The final count is sometimes below 800 000.
questions.stem: Why, and what fixes it?
options: Dict assignment is never atomic; switch to a list
The += is a read-modify-write that can interleave between threads; guard it with a threading.Lock
The GIL was released by the dict; call sys.setswitchinterval(0)
Threads cannot share dicts; use separate dicts and assume the totals match
questions.explanation: The GIL keeps single bytecodes atomic, but `stats['hits'] += 1` reads, adds and stores in separate steps, so two threads can read the same value. The Library FAQ lists `D[x] = D[x] + 1` as not atomic; a lock makes the update atomic.
rationales: A single D[x] = y is atomic in CPython; the read-modify-write is the problem.
Correct: lock the compound update.
The switch interval cannot be zero and does not make compound operations atomic.
Threads can share dicts; per-thread counters would need a final merge, not an assumption.

questions.scenario: A producer thread parses log lines and several consumer threads write them to a database. The producer must slow down when consumers fall behind.
questions.stem: Which design fits best?
options: A shared list with append and pop(0), plus time.sleep polling
A queue.Queue with maxsize set, consumers calling get() and task_done()
An asyncio.Queue shared between the threads
A global variable protected by the GIL
questions.explanation: queue.Queue is a thread-safe FIFO with locking built in, and a maxsize makes put() block when full, giving back-pressure. asyncio.Queue is not thread-safe.
rationales: Polling wastes CPU and pop(0) is O(n); there is no back-pressure.
Correct: thread-safe hand-off with blocking put for back-pressure.
asyncio.Queue is meant for tasks in one event loop, not threads.
The GIL does not make a hand-off protocol safe.

questions.scenario: A helper takes a threading.Lock and then calls another helper that also takes the same lock, on the same thread. The program freezes.
questions.stem: What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch to asyncio.Lock
Use threading.Event instead of a lock
Call lock.release() before acquiring
Use threading.RLock, which the owning thread can re-acquire
questions.explanation: threading.Lock is not reentrant, so acquiring it again from the thread that holds it blocks forever. RLock tracks the owner and a recursion count, so nested acquires by the same thread succeed.
rationales: asyncio.Lock is for coroutines and is not thread-safe.
Event signals a flag; it does not provide mutual exclusion.
Releasing a lock you need for the outer section breaks its protection.
Correct: RLock is reentrant.

questions.scenario: A team reviews a thread-pool design for a CPython 3.13 service.
questions.stem: Which statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: list.append from several threads on a shared list is atomic in CPython
x += 1 on a shared int is atomic because of the GIL
Correct code should not rely on the GIL, because builds without it exist
queue.Queue.join() returns when the queue is empty, even without task_done() calls
questions.explanation: The Library FAQ lists L.append(x) among operations atomic in CPython, while x += 1 is a read-modify-write. The free-threaded build (experimental in 3.13) removes the GIL, so relying on it is fragile. Queue.join waits for a task_done for every item.
rationales: Correct: listed as atomic in CPython.
It is not atomic; updates can be lost.
Correct: free-threaded builds remove the GIL.
join waits until every put item has had task_done called.

questions.scenario: A background thread receives messages from a socket and must hand each one to a coroutine running on the main thread's event loop.
questions.stem: Which call should the thread use?
options: asyncio.run(handle(msg))
asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(handle(msg), loop)
loop.create_task(handle(msg)) called from the thread
asyncio.to_thread(handle, msg)
questions.explanation: The event loop is not thread-safe, so other threads must use the threadsafe APIs. run_coroutine_threadsafe schedules the coroutine on the given loop and returns a concurrent.futures.Future the thread can wait on.
rationales: That would start a second, separate event loop in the thread.
Correct: the documented way to submit a coroutine from another thread.
create_task is not thread-safe when called from another thread.
to_thread goes the other way, running a function in a thread from the loop.

questions.scenario: A helper `def total_area(shapes: list[Shape]) -> float` only reads its argument. A caller passes a `list[Circle]`, where `Circle` subclasses `Shape`, and the static checker flags the call even though the code works.
questions.stem: What is the best change to the signature?
options: Add `# type: ignore` at every call site.
Declare a `TypeVar("T", covariant=True)` and annotate the parameter as `list[T]`.
Change the parameter to `Sequence[Shape]` (or `Iterable[Shape]`), which is covariant for read-only use.
Change the parameter to `list[Any]` so any list is accepted.
questions.explanation: list is invariant because it is mutable: a function that receives `list[Shape]` could append a non-circle shape to the caller's `list[Circle]`. Read-only abstract types such as Sequence are covariant, so accepting them is the idiomatic fix.
rationales: Silencing the checker at call sites spreads the problem instead of fixing the signature.
list stays invariant regardless of the TypeVar; variance belongs to the generic class, not the argument.
Correct: Sequence is covariant, so a sequence of a subtype is accepted for read-only use.
This discards the element type and hides real errors.

questions.scenario: A team on Python 3.13 is modernising `T = TypeVar("T")` / `class Stack(Generic[T])` code.
questions.stem: Which rewrite uses the PEP 695 syntax correctly?
options: `class Stack(Generic[T]):` with `T` declared as `type T = TypeVar()`.
`class Stack<T>:` with methods annotated using `T`.
`@generic(T) class Stack:` with methods annotated using `T`.
`class Stack[T]:` with methods annotated using `T`, and no TypeVar or Generic import.
questions.explanation: PEP 695 (3.12) adds a bracketed type-parameter list to `class` and `def` statements, which replaces the module-level TypeVar and the Generic base. The other spellings are not Python syntax or misuse the `type` statement.
rationales: The `type` statement declares aliases, not type variables.
Angle brackets are not Python syntax.
There is no `@generic` decorator in typing.
Correct: this is the 3.12+ type-parameter syntax.

questions.scenario: A module on 3.13 defines `type Tree = dict[str, Tree] | Leaf` near the top, and `Leaf` is defined further down the file.
questions.stem: What happens when the module is imported?
options: It imports fine, because the alias value is evaluated lazily when `Tree.__value__` is first accessed.
It raises NameError at the `type` statement because `Leaf` is not defined yet.
It raises SyntaxError because an alias cannot refer to itself.
It imports, but `Tree` is a plain `types.UnionType` evaluated immediately.
questions.explanation: The `type` statement creates a TypeAliasType whose value is computed lazily, so forward and recursive references work without quotes. This contrasts with 3.13 function annotations, which are still evaluated eagerly.
rationales: Correct: the value is evaluated on demand.
That would be true of an ordinary assignment, not of a `type` alias.
Recursive aliases are allowed and are one motivation for lazy evaluation.
The result is a TypeAliasType, and its value is not evaluated at definition.

questions.stem: Which statements about variance are correct? (Select two.)
options: Callable parameter types are covariant.
A plain `TypeVar("T")` with no flags is invariant.
Type parameters declared with PEP 695 syntax have their variance inferred from usage.
`list` is covariant, so `list[bool]` is accepted where `list[int]` is expected.
questions.explanation: Old-style TypeVars are invariant unless declared covariant or contravariant, while PEP 695 parameters get inferred variance. list is invariant and callable parameter types are contravariant.
rationales: Callable parameters are contravariant: a callback accepting a wider type is acceptable.
Correct: invariant is the default for TypeVar.
Correct: PEP 695 introduced variance inference.
list is mutable and therefore invariant.

questions.scenario: A plugin loader accepts any object with a `run(self) -> None` method. Third-party plugins cannot be changed to inherit from a base class.
questions.stem: Which approach fits best for static typing?
options: Annotate the parameter as `object` and call `run` through `getattr`.
Annotate the parameter as `Any`.
Define a `typing.Protocol` with `run(self) -> None` and annotate the parameter with it.
Define an ABC with an abstract `run` and require plugins to subclass it.
questions.explanation: Protocols (PEP 544) give structural subtyping: any class with a compatible `run` satisfies the type without inheriting. An ABC is nominal and would force the plugins to change.
rationales: This loses all checking of the `run` method.
Any disables checking entirely.
Correct: structural typing matches the constraint.
ABCs require inheritance or registration, which the plugins cannot do.

questions.scenario: A service validates input with `isinstance(obj, Handler)`, where `Handler` is a `@runtime_checkable` Protocol requiring `def handle(self, req: Request) -> Response`. An object whose `handle` attribute is the string "todo" passes the check and fails later.
questions.stem: Why did it pass?
options: runtime_checkable caches the first successful check and reuses it.
Protocols are only checked at import time.
The check fell back to duck typing because `Request` is not runtime_checkable.
Runtime protocol checks only verify that the members exist, not their types or signatures.
questions.explanation: The typing docs state that isinstance against a runtime-checkable protocol checks only for the presence of the required attributes. It is a coarse structural filter, so real validation must call or inspect the member.
rationales: No such caching behaviour exists.
The isinstance check runs when called, not at import.
Parameter annotations are not consulted at all.
Correct: presence-only checking is documented behaviour.

questions.scenario: An API client parses JSON into `class User(TypedDict): id: int; name: str`. A teammate adds `if not isinstance(data, User): raise ValueError` to validate responses.
questions.stem: What happens?
options: The check always returns True because every TypedDict instance is a dict.
The check works and rejects dicts whose values have the wrong types.
The check works but only verifies that the keys exist.
`isinstance` raises TypeError, because TypedDict does not support instance checks; runtime validation needs explicit code or a validation library.
questions.explanation: A TypedDict is a static description; at runtime instances are plain dicts and isinstance with a TypedDict raises TypeError. Validating untrusted JSON needs explicit checks.
rationales: The call raises rather than returning a result.
Values are never checked at runtime.
Keys are not checked either; the call raises before any checking.
Correct: TypedDict does not support isinstance.

questions.scenario: A function `load(path, raw: bool)` returns `bytes` when `raw=True` and `str` otherwise. Callers want precise return types.
questions.stem: Which approach gives the checker per-call return types?
options: A `TypeVar("T", bytes, str)` return type with no parameter using `T`.
Two `@overload` signatures using `Literal[True]` and `Literal[False]` for `raw`, followed by one undecorated implementation.
A return annotation of `bytes | str`.
Two separate implementations decorated with `@overload` that each contain real logic.
questions.explanation: Overloads combined with Literal types let a checker select the return type from the argument value. Only the final undecorated definition runs, so overload stubs should just contain `...`.
rationales: A TypeVar that appears only in the return type cannot be solved from the arguments.
Correct: overload plus Literal is the documented pattern.
A union forces every caller to narrow the result themselves.
Overloaded stubs are replaced by the implementation; their bodies never run.

questions.scenario: A logging decorator is typed `def logged(f: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]`. After applying it, the IDE no longer flags wrong arguments to decorated functions.
questions.stem: Which change restores checking of the wrapped signature?
options: Annotate the return as `Self`.
Change `Callable[..., Any]` to `Callable[[Any], Any]`.
Use a ParamSpec: `def logged[**P, R](f: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]`, with the wrapper taking `*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs`.
Add `functools.wraps(f)` to the wrapper; it copies the type signature for checkers.
questions.explanation: ParamSpec (3.10) captures the full parameter list of a callable so a decorator can return a callable with the same parameters. functools.wraps copies runtime metadata such as `__name__` and `__wrapped__`, not static types.
rationales: Self is for methods returning their own class.
That restricts the function to one argument and still loses the real signature.
Correct: ParamSpec is designed for signature-preserving decorators.
wraps affects runtime attributes, not what a static checker infers.

questions.scenario: A dataclass `Order` has `items: list = []`. The module fails to import.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: `items: list = list()`
`items: list = None` and leave it as None
`items: list = [].copy()`
`items: list = field(default_factory=list)`
questions.explanation: Since 3.11, dataclasses reject unhashable defaults (which covers list, dict and set) with a ValueError that recommends default_factory. A factory is called per instance, so instances do not share one list.
rationales: This is still a single list object evaluated once, and is rejected the same way.
This avoids the error but changes the type and forces None checks everywhere.
Still one shared list created at class definition, and still rejected.
Correct: default_factory creates a new list for each instance.

questions.scenario: A cache uses `seen: set[Point]`, where `Point` is `@dataclass class Point: x: int; y: int`. `seen.add(Point(1, 2))` raises `TypeError: unhashable type`.
questions.stem: What is the cleanest fix if points never change after creation?
options: Use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, which generates a field-based `__hash__`.
Add `__hash__ = object.__hash__` to the class.
Use `@dataclass(eq=False)` so the default identity hash returns.
Use `@dataclass(order=True)`.
questions.explanation: With eq=True and frozen=False, dataclass sets `__hash__` to None, so instances are unhashable. frozen=True plus eq=True generates a hash consistent with equality and prevents mutation that would break it.
rationales: Correct: frozen makes value-based hashing safe and automatic.
Identity hashing with value equality breaks the hash/eq contract: equal points would hash differently.
This hashes by identity, so two equal-looking points are distinct set members.
Ordering methods do not affect hashability.

questions.scenario: A frozen dataclass `Email(address: str)` should store the address lower-cased. The author writes `self.address = self.address.lower()` in `__post_init__`.
questions.stem: What happens, and what is the documented fix?
options: It silently does nothing; use `dataclasses.replace` inside `__post_init__`.
FrozenInstanceError is raised; use `object.__setattr__(self, "address", self.address.lower())`.
It works because `__post_init__` runs before the instance is frozen.
AttributeError is raised; add `slots=True` to fix it.
questions.explanation: Frozen dataclasses block assignment through the generated `__setattr__`, including inside `__post_init__`. The dataclasses docs describe calling `object.__setattr__` as the workaround.
rationales: The assignment raises; replace would build a new object that `__init__` cannot return.
Correct: the generated `__setattr__` raises and object.__setattr__ bypasses it.
The frozen check applies from the start, including in `__post_init__`.
slots does not lift the frozen restriction.

questions.scenario: A team chooses between `class P(NamedTuple): x: int; y: int` and `@dataclass(frozen=True) class P: x: int; y: int` for API result records.
questions.stem: Which statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: Both versions raise FrozenInstanceError on assignment.
Only the dataclass version can have default values.
The NamedTuple version compares equal to a plain tuple `(1, 2)`; the dataclass version does not.
The NamedTuple version supports unpacking and indexing like a tuple.
questions.explanation: NamedTuple creates a tuple subclass, so it indexes, unpacks and compares like a tuple. A dataclass `__eq__` only compares with instances of the same class, and NamedTuple assignment raises AttributeError, not FrozenInstanceError.
rationales: NamedTuple raises AttributeError; only dataclasses use FrozenInstanceError.
NamedTuple fields can have defaults too.
Correct: tuple equality is inherited.
Correct: it is a tuple subclass.

questions.scenario: A status dispatcher has `OK = 200` at module level and the code `match code: case OK: ...  case _: ...`. It fails to compile.
questions.stem: Why, and what is the fix?
options: `match` cannot compare integers; convert `code` to a string.
Module constants must be declared `Final` to be used in case clauses.
The wildcard `_` must come first.
A bare name is a capture pattern that matches anything, which makes later cases unreachable; use a dotted name such as `Status.OK` or a literal.
questions.explanation: In a case clause a bare name binds the subject instead of comparing to it. Because it is irrefutable, any case after it is unreachable and Python raises SyntaxError; value patterns must be dotted names.
rationales: Integer literals are valid patterns.
Final has no effect on pattern semantics.
A leading wildcard would make every other case unreachable.
Correct: dotted names are value patterns and compare by equality.

questions.scenario: An event router matches `case {"type": "click", "x": x, "y": y}:`. An event `{"type": "click", "x": 1, "y": 2, "button": "right"}` arrives.
questions.stem: What happens?
options: It matches only if the case adds a `**_` entry.
It does not match, because mapping patterns require an exact key set.
It raises TypeError, because dict subjects need a `**rest` pattern.
It matches; mapping patterns ignore extra keys, so `button` is not checked.
questions.explanation: Mapping patterns succeed when the listed keys are present and their sub-patterns match; additional keys are ignored. Use `**rest` to capture extras or a guard to reject them.
rationales: `**_` is not even allowed; the extra keys are ignored by default.
No exact-shape requirement exists for mappings.
No error is raised for extra keys.
Correct: subset matching is the documented rule.

questions.scenario: A dataclass `Point(x: int, y: int)` is matched with `case Point(0, y):`.
questions.stem: Why can positional sub-patterns be used here?
options: Positional patterns work only for NamedTuples, so this raises TypeError.
The dataclass generates `__match_args__ = ("x", "y")`, which maps positions to attributes.
Class patterns always map positions to `__init__` parameters.
Class patterns compare against the object's tuple form.
questions.explanation: Positional sub-patterns in a class pattern are resolved through the class's `__match_args__`. Dataclasses generate it from their fields by default; other classes must define it.
rationales: Dataclasses support positional class patterns.
Correct: `__match_args__` drives positional matching.
The interpreter does not inspect `__init__` for this.
Objects are not converted to tuples for matching.

questions.scenario: An API returns `{"status": 2}`, and the code defines `class Status(Enum): ACTIVE = 2`. The check `if payload["status"] == Status.ACTIVE:` is never true.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Add `@enum.unique` to the class.
Compare with `Status.ACTIVE.name`.
Convert the raw value with `Status(payload["status"])` before comparing (or use IntEnum if int interoperability is intended).
Compare with `is` instead of `==`.
questions.explanation: Plain Enum members do not compare equal to their raw values. Calling the enum with a value looks up the member, and IntEnum members are designed to compare equal to ints.
rationales: unique only rejects duplicate values.
The name is the string "ACTIVE", which does not equal 2.
Correct: value lookup or IntEnum solves the mismatch.
An int is never the same object as an Enum member.

questions.scenario: A `@contextmanager` generator acquires a lock, does `yield`, then releases the lock on the next line. When the with-body raises, the lock stays held.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Return True after the release so the exception is suppressed.
Replace `yield` with `return`.
Catch BaseException around the with statement in every caller.
Wrap the `yield` in `try: ... finally:` and release the lock in the `finally` block.
questions.explanation: contextmanager re-raises the body's exception inside the generator at the yield point. Without try/finally the code after yield never runs, so cleanup must be in a finally block.
rationales: Suppressing errors hides failures and does not move the cleanup.
A contextmanager generator must yield exactly once.
This pushes cleanup to every caller and does not release the lock.
Correct: finally runs whether or not the body raises.

questions.scenario: A library wraps low-level errors: `except OSError as e: raise ConfigError("cannot read config")`. Reviewers want the traceback to show the OSError explicitly as the cause, and callers to be able to catch all library failures in one place.
questions.stem: Which changes meet both goals? (Select two.)
options: Use `raise ConfigError("cannot read config") from e`.
Make ConfigError subclass a single library base exception such as `MyLibError`.
Use `raise ConfigError("cannot read config") from None`.
Catch `Exception` instead of `OSError` so every error becomes a ConfigError.
questions.explanation: `raise ... from e` sets `__cause__`, producing the "direct cause" traceback. A shared base exception lets callers catch every library error with one except clause, while `from None` hides the original.
rationales: Correct: explicit chaining records the cause.
Correct: a library base exception supports broad catching.
This suppresses the context, the opposite of the goal.
Over-broad catching mislabels unrelated bugs as config errors.

questions.scenario: A custom context manager class always ends `__exit__` with `return True` "to be safe". Bugs inside `with` blocks go unnoticed in production.
questions.stem: Why?
options: Returning True converts exceptions into warnings.
A true return value from `__exit__` tells Python to suppress the exception raised in the with-body.
`return True` makes `__exit__` run twice.
`__exit__` must return the exception object to re-raise it.
questions.explanation: When `__exit__` returns a true value, the exception is swallowed and execution continues after the with statement. Return None or False unless suppression is intended; for deliberate suppression of specific types, use `contextlib.suppress`.
rationales: No conversion to warnings occurs.
Correct: truthy return means suppress.
The return value does not affect how often `__exit__` runs.
Returning a falsy value is enough to propagate the exception.

questions.scenario: A worker reads jobs into a Python list and processes them in arrival order with `job = jobs.pop(0)`. With 500,000 queued jobs, throughput collapses as the backlog grows.
questions.stem: Which change best fixes the scaling problem while keeping first-in, first-out order?
options: Convert the list to a `set` and take jobs with `set.pop()`.
Keep the list but add new jobs with `insert(0, job)` and take them with `pop()`.
Store the jobs in a `collections.deque` and take each job with `popleft()`.
Call `jobs.sort()` before each `pop(0)` so the list stays compact.
questions.explanation: In CPython, `list.pop(0)` is O(n) because every remaining element shifts, so draining a long queue is quadratic. A deque supports appends and pops at both ends in about O(1), which makes it the standard FIFO queue.
rationales: Sets are unordered and drop duplicates, so FIFO order is lost.
Moving the cost does not remove it: `insert(0, x)` is also O(n).
Correct: `deque.popleft()` is O(1) and preserves FIFO order.
Sorting adds O(n log n) work per job and does not change the cost of `pop(0)`.

questions.scenario: A deduplication step loops over 2 million incoming IDs and skips any ID already processed, using `if id_ in seen: continue` followed by `seen.append(id_)`, where `seen` is a list.
questions.stem: Why does this step slow down so sharply as input grows, and what is the fix?
options: Python caches the list on every append; call `gc.collect()` every 10,000 iterations.
List appends are O(n) because the list is copied on every append; preallocate the list with `[None] * n`.
The `continue` statement forces the loop to restart; replace it with an `else` branch.
Each `in` check scans the list in O(n), making the loop quadratic; make `seen` a `set` so membership is O(1) on average.
questions.explanation: Membership in a list is a linear scan, so checking every new ID against a growing list costs O(n²) overall. Sets and dicts are hash tables with average O(1) membership, which turns the loop back into roughly linear time.
rationales: Garbage collection is unrelated to the cost of a linear membership scan.
CPython lists over-allocate, so appends are amortised O(1); preallocation would not fix the scan.
`continue` just skips to the next iteration and is not a cost.
Correct: the linear membership test is the bottleneck, and a set removes it.

questions.scenario: A report generator builds a 50 MB CSV string with `out += row_text` for each of several hundred thousand rows. A teammate says this is fine because "CPython optimises string +=".
questions.stem: What is the most reliable approach?
options: Keep `+=`, since the optimisation is guaranteed by the language specification.
Append each row to a list and call `"".join(rows)` once at the end.
Use `out = out + row_text` instead, because it avoids creating new strings.
Convert `out` to a `bytes` object, since bytes concatenation is in-place.
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, and the docs warn that repeatedly concatenating immutable sequences can have quadratic runtime cost. Any in-place optimisation is a CPython detail that is easy to defeat, so `str.join` (or `io.StringIO`) is the reliable pattern.
rationales: The behaviour is an implementation detail, not a language guarantee.
Correct: join builds the result in one pass with linear cost.
`out = out + x` still creates a new string every time and is the same problem.
`bytes` is also immutable; `bytearray` would be mutable, but bytes concatenation is not in-place.

questions.scenario: An engineer uses `timeit` to compare two functions that both create millions of short-lived objects, many in reference cycles. The benchmark says version B is 20% faster, but in production B is slower.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of the mismatch?
options: `timeit` reports the mean of all runs, which is skewed by the first, cold run.
`timeit` measures CPU time only, so time spent in memory allocation is excluded.
`timeit` runs the snippet in a separate process with a different interpreter version.
`timeit` disables garbage collection during timing by default, so the cost of collecting B's cycles was not measured.
questions.explanation: By default `timeit` temporarily turns off garbage collection, which makes timings more comparable but can hide GC cost that matters in production. The docs show re-enabling it by passing `gc.enable()` as the first setup statement.
rationales: `timeit()` returns a total, and the docs recommend taking the minimum of `repeat()`, not the mean.
The default timer is `time.perf_counter()`, a wall-clock timer, and allocation time is included.
`timeit` runs in the current interpreter, not a separate process.
Correct: GC is off during timing unless you enable it in setup.

questions.scenario: An API endpoint takes 4 seconds. A developer is sure the JSON serialisation is to blame and plans to rewrite it as a C extension.
questions.stem: What should happen first?
options: Add `@functools.lru_cache` to every function in the request path.
Start the C rewrite, because serialisation is usually the slowest part of an API.
Run the endpoint under `cProfile`, sort the stats by cumulative time with `pstats`, and optimise what the profile shows.
Time `json.dumps` alone with `timeit` and assume the rest of the request is negligible.
questions.explanation: Optimising without measuring often targets the wrong code. `cProfile` records every call with counts and cumulative times, so it shows where the 4 seconds actually go before you invest in a fix.
rationales: Blanket caching can be incorrect for impure functions and adds memory without evidence.
A rewrite based on a guess may not touch the real bottleneck.
Correct: profile the real workload, then change the top hotspot.
A micro-benchmark of one function cannot tell you its share of the full request.

questions.scenario: A long-running service's memory grows by about 200 MB per hour. Restarting fixes it temporarily. You need to know which source lines are responsible for the growth.
questions.stem: Which approach finds them most directly with the standard library?
options: Call `gc.collect()` periodically and log how many objects it returns.
Run the service under `cProfile` and look for functions with the highest cumulative time.
Call `sys.getsizeof()` on the main objects every few minutes and log the results.
Start `tracemalloc`, take a snapshot, let the service run, take another snapshot, and call `compare_to(first, "lineno")`.
questions.explanation: `tracemalloc` records where each traced block was allocated, and comparing two snapshots groups the difference by line, which points at the code holding on to memory. The other tools measure time, shallow sizes or cycle collection, not where growth comes from.
rationales: The collected count shows cycle garbage, not the lines that allocate retained memory.
`cProfile` measures time spent, not memory retained.
`getsizeof` is shallow and does not say where memory was allocated.
Correct: snapshot comparison by line is the documented way to find leaks.

questions.stem: Which two statements about measuring code with `timeit` are correct? (Select two.)
options: When using `repeat()`, the minimum result is the most useful figure, because higher values are usually caused by interference.
Garbage collection is turned off during timing unless the setup re-enables it.
The default timer measures process CPU time, so sleeping or waiting on I/O is excluded.
Reporting the mean and standard deviation of `repeat()` is the recommended way to summarise results.
questions.explanation: The timeit docs recommend looking at the minimum of `repeat()` and note that GC is disabled during timing by default. The default timer is `time.perf_counter()`, which is wall-clock time, and the docs say the mean and standard deviation are not very useful.
rationales: Correct: the lowest value gives a lower bound for how fast the code can run.
Correct: GC is disabled by default; add `gc.enable()` to setup to include it.
Incorrect: `perf_counter()` is a wall-clock timer, so waiting time is counted.
Incorrect: the docs explicitly say the mean and standard deviation are not very useful here.

questions.scenario: `app/report.py` contains `from app.clock import now` and uses `now()` to stamp reports. A test does `with mock.patch("app.clock.now", return_value=FIXED): build_report()`, but the report still carries the real current time.
questions.stem: What change makes the patch take effect?
options: Patch `"datetime.datetime.now"` because `now` probably calls it.
Patch `"app.report.now"`, the name the code under test actually looks up.
Add `autospec=True` to the existing patch of `"app.clock.now"`.
Import `app.report` after entering the patch context, inside the test.
questions.explanation: The `from ... import` copied a reference to `now` into the `app.report` namespace, so patching `app.clock.now` replaces a name `build_report` never reads. The mock docs' rule is to patch where an object is looked up, which here is `app.report.now`.
rationales: Built-in types like `datetime.datetime` cannot have attributes set, and this does not target the reference the code uses.
Correct: this replaces the reference `build_report` actually calls.
autospec checks signatures; it does not change which namespace is patched.
If `app.report` was already imported elsewhere, it is cached in `sys.modules` and not re-executed, so this is fragile at best.

questions.scenario: You are testing `async def load(client)`, which does `data = await client.get("/status")`. A test passes `client = mock.MagicMock()` with `client.get.return_value = {"ok": True}`, and the test fails with a TypeError when `load` runs.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Use `mock.AsyncMock()` for the client so `client.get(...)` returns an awaitable, and check it with `assert_awaited_once_with("/status")`.
Wrap the return value in a list so MagicMock treats it as awaitable.
Set `client.get.side_effect = {"ok": True}`.
Call `load(client)` without awaiting it, so the mock is never awaited.
questions.explanation: Calling a MagicMock returns another MagicMock, which cannot be awaited, so `await` raises TypeError. `AsyncMock` returns an awaitable whose result is `return_value`, and it offers await-specific assertions.
rationales: Correct: AsyncMock is designed for awaited calls.
A list is not awaitable either.
A dict `side_effect` is treated as an iterable of successive return values, and the result is still not awaitable.
Not awaiting `load` returns a coroutine object and never runs the code under test.

questions.scenario: Several tests need a temporary database connection that must be closed after each test, even when the test fails. Currently every test opens and closes it by hand, and a failing assertion leaks connections.
questions.stem: Which pytest approach fits best?
options: A helper function each test calls at its start, with `close()` as the test's last line.
A module-level global connection opened at import time and never closed.
A `@pytest.fixture` that opens the connection, `yield`s it, and closes it after the `yield`; tests request it by parameter name.
Mark each test with `@pytest.mark.parametrize("db", [connect()])`.
questions.explanation: A yield fixture puts setup before the `yield` and teardown after it, and pytest runs the teardown even if the test fails. Tests receive the value just by naming the fixture as a parameter.
rationales: A failing assertion stops the test before its last line, so the connection leaks.
A shared global leaks state between tests and is never cleaned up.
Correct: yield fixtures give guaranteed teardown and reuse.
parametrize evaluates the value at collection time and has no teardown step.

sources.title: How to use fixtures — pytest docs

questions.scenario: A test checks a parser against 30 input/expected pairs by looping over them inside one test function. When it fails, the report shows a single failure and the team cannot tell how many cases are broken.
questions.stem: What is the better design?
options: Wrap each assertion in `try/except AssertionError` and print failures.
Use `@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, expected", cases)` so each pair runs and reports as its own test.
Split the cases across 30 copy-pasted test functions.
Use a fixture that returns the whole list of cases.
questions.explanation: parametrize generates one test per argument set, so every case is run and reported separately. A loop inside one test stops at the first failing assertion.
rationales: Swallowing assertions can make the test pass while cases are broken.
Correct: each case becomes an independently reported test.
Copy-pasting works but is hard to maintain; parametrize does this for you.
A fixture returning a list still leaves a loop inside one test.

questions.scenario: Production crashed with `AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'sendd'`, yet the unit test for that code path passed. The test used `mock.patch("app.notify.Client")` with no other options.
questions.stem: What change would have made the test catch the bug?
options: Set `return_value=None` on the patch.
Replace `Mock` with `MagicMock`, which validates attribute names.
Assert `client.sendd.assert_called_once()` to confirm the call happened.
Patch with `autospec=True` (or use `create_autospec(Client)`) so the mock only allows attributes and signatures the real class has.
questions.explanation: A plain Mock creates any attribute on access, so `sendd` silently succeeds. Autospeccing builds the mock from the real object, so a missing attribute raises AttributeError and a bad call signature raises TypeError.
rationales: `return_value` controls what the call returns, not which attributes exist.
MagicMock adds magic methods but still accepts any attribute name.
That assertion would pass and confirm the wrong behaviour.
Correct: autospec makes the mock as strict as the real API.

questions.scenario: A package `mytool` has a function `main()` in `mytool/cli.py`. Users should be able to run `mytool` from the shell after `pip install`.
questions.stem: What belongs in `pyproject.toml`?
options: `[project.scripts]` with `mytool = "mytool.cli:main"`.
`[project.entry-points.console_scripts]` with `mytool = "mytool.cli:main"`.
`[build-system]` with `requires = ["mytool.cli:main"]`.
A `scripts = ["mytool/cli.py"]` key under `[project]`, pointing at the file.
questions.explanation: PEP 621 defines `[project.scripts]` for console commands as `name = "module:function"`. Installers create an executable that imports the module and calls the function.
rationales: Correct: this is the standard console-script declaration.
PEP 621 forbids declaring console_scripts through the generic entry-points table; use `[project.scripts]`.
`[build-system].requires` lists build-time dependencies, not commands.
`[project]` has no file-based scripts key; scripts map names to object references.

questions.scenario: An internal library declares `dependencies = ["requests==2.31.0", "pydantic==2.6.1"]`. Teams that install it next to other packages keep hitting resolver conflicts.
questions.stem: What is the recommended practice?
options: Keep the exact pins and ask every consuming team to use the same versions.
In the library, declare compatible minimum versions or ranges; let each application pin exact versions in its own lock or requirements file.
Remove all dependencies from the library and document them in the README.
Vendor copies of both dependencies inside the library package.
questions.explanation: Abstract requirements in a library should be as loose as correctness allows so they can coexist with other packages. Exact, repeatable pins belong to the deployed application, typically in a requirements or lock file.
rationales: Exact pins in a library force every consumer onto one version and cause conflicts.
Correct: ranges for libraries, exact pins for applications.
Undeclared dependencies break installs and are not resolved automatically.
Vendoring adds maintenance and security burden and is not the standard fix.

questions.stem: Which two statements about virtual environments created with `python -m venv` are correct? (Select two.)
options: The environment has its own `site-packages` directory, isolated from the base interpreter's packages.
The environment directory can be copied to another path or machine and used as-is.
Inside the environment, `sys.prefix` differs from `sys.base_prefix`.
The environment cannot be used until its activation script has been run.
questions.explanation: A venv has its own independent set of installed packages, and when Python runs from one, `sys.prefix` points at the venv while `sys.base_prefix` points at the base install. The docs say environments are not movable or copyable and that activation is optional: you can run the environment's interpreter by path.
rationales: Correct: isolation of installed packages is the purpose of a venv.
Incorrect: the docs say venvs are not considered movable or copyable; recreate them instead.
Correct: this is how code detects it is running in a venv.
Incorrect: running the venv's python by its path works without activation.

questions.scenario: A library exposes `def fetch(url, timeout, retries, verify)`. Call sites like `fetch(u, 5, 3, False)` are unreadable, and the maintainers want to add new options later without breaking callers.
questions.stem: Which signature best supports this?
options: `def fetch(url, timeout=10, retries=3, verify=True, /)`
`def fetch(*args)` and unpack the options by position inside
`def fetch(url, *, timeout=10, retries=3, verify=True)`
`def fetch(url, options)` where `options` is a tuple in a documented order
questions.explanation: Parameters after a bare `*` are keyword-only (PEP 3102), so callers must name them, which makes calls readable and lets maintainers add or reorder options safely. A trailing `/` would do the opposite and force positional use.
rationales: `/` makes every parameter positional-only, keeping the unreadable calls.
Positional unpacking hides meaning and makes changes break callers.
Correct: keyword-only options are explicit at call sites.
An ordered tuple has the same readability and ordering problems.

questions.scenario: You are renaming `parse_cfg()` to `load_config()` in a widely used library. The old name must keep working for a while. In a first attempt, the warning output points at a line inside your library, so users cannot tell which of their calls need updating.
questions.stem: Which implementation of the old name is best?
options: Raise `DeprecationWarning` as an exception from `parse_cfg()`.
Delete `parse_cfg()` now and mention the rename in the changelog.
Call `print("deprecated")` and delegate to `load_config()`.
Call `warnings.warn("parse_cfg() is deprecated; use load_config()", DeprecationWarning, stacklevel=2)` and then delegate to `load_config()`.
questions.explanation: `stacklevel=2` makes the warning refer to the caller's line, which tells users exactly what to change, while delegation keeps old code working during the deprecation period. Removing APIs abruptly or raising breaks callers, and print cannot be filtered or turned into errors in CI.
rationales: Raising turns the deprecation into an immediate break.
Removing without a deprecation period breaks every existing caller.
print bypasses the warnings machinery, so it cannot be filtered or made an error.
Correct: a filterable DeprecationWarning attributed to the caller.

questions.stem: A module defines `__all__ = ["load", "save"]` and also a function `_cache_key` and a public-looking function `migrate`. Which two statements are correct? (Select two.)
options: `from module import *` imports `load` and `save` but not `migrate`.
`from module import migrate` raises ImportError because `migrate` is not in `__all__`.
`from module import _cache_key` works, because `__all__` does not hide names.
Accessing `module.migrate` raises AttributeError.
questions.explanation: `__all__` lists the names a star import binds, so only `load` and `save` come in. It has no effect on explicit imports or attribute access, so `migrate` and `_cache_key` stay reachable.
rationales: Correct: star import uses `__all__` when it is defined.
Incorrect: explicit imports of unlisted names still work.
Correct: underscores and `__all__` are conventions, not access control.
Incorrect: the attribute still exists on the module.

questions.scenario: A maths library has `def clamp(value, low, high)`. The maintainers want to rename `value` to `x` in a future release, but some users call `clamp(value=5, low=0, high=10)`.
questions.stem: If the library had used one of these signatures from its first release, which one would have let the parameters be renamed later without breaking any caller?
options: `def clamp(value, low, high, /)`
`def clamp(*, value, low, high)`
`def clamp(value, low, high, **kwargs)`
`def clamp(value=None, low=None, high=None)`
questions.explanation: Parameters before `/` are positional-only (PEP 570), so callers cannot pass them by name and their names are not part of the public API. Keyword-only parameters do the opposite and make the names permanent.
rationales: Correct: positional-only names can change freely.
Keyword-only parameters force callers to use the names, locking them in.
`**kwargs` still allows `value=` to bind by name.
Defaults do not prevent keyword calls, so the names remain public.
